items.title: Climate Misinformation and Media Literacy: A Case Study of Rwanda: A Research Paper
items.source_name: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: This paper examines climate misinformation through the case of Rwanda, a country combining high climate vulnerability with a tightly regulated media environment. Drawing on climate science, disaster response, and media-freedom literature, alongside Rwanda-specific data on digital access, literacy, and misinformation literacy from adjacent COVID-19 research, the paper argues that Rwanda's information-control approach appears to reduce measured public exposure to misinformation without a clear basis for concluding that it reduces underlying vulnerability. The analysis further shows that Rwanda's low overall internet and social media penetration, combined with a pronounced urban-rural digital divide, means that radio, community networks, and closed messaging channels such as WhatsApp are likely more consequential vectors for climate misinformation among the agricultural populations most exposed to climate risk than the open social media platforms that dominate existing misinformation research. The paper concludes by identifying the need to measure climate misinformation exposure directly in Rwanda, an evidence gaps the existing literature has not yet filled.

items.title: Prioritizing demand-side use of clean hydrogen for cost-effective mitigation
Research attitudes through the COVID-19 pandemic
items.summary_raw: Introduction Identifying the factors that influence attitudes toward biomedical research is essential for improving public engagement and participation. The COVID-19 pandemic offers a unique opportunity to assess how a public health crisis shapes perceptions of clinical research. We investigated whether attitudes toward biomedical research differed across phases of the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods We analyzed data from 5,098 adults enrolled in the UC Irvine Consent-to-Contact (C2C) registry, an online voluntary recruitment registry in Southern California, between June 2016 and August 2025. Research attitudes were assessed with the validated 7-item Research Attitudes Questionnaire (RAQ) at enrollment and annually thereafter. Scores were analyzed continuously (7 -35) and dichotomously, with >28 defined a priori as high. COVID-19 periods were defined a priori as: P1 (before March 13, 2020—the U.S. national emergency declaration), P2 (March 13 to December 11, 2020—prior to COVID-19 vaccine approval), and P3 (after December 11, 2020—post-vaccine approval). Cross-sectional analyses included all participants; longitudinal analyses were limited to 1,388 participants who enrolled before March 2020 and had ≥3 assessments. Results Our sample of 5,098 adults was predominantly non-Hispanic White (70.2%), female (65.7%), highly educated, and over age 50 (66.7%). Participants enrolling during P2 had 60% higher odds of a high RAQ score (>28) compared with P1 (aOR 1.60; 95% CI: 1.07, 2.40; p…

items.title: Awareness, persuasion, and willingness to purchase: a study on taxi drivers’ preferences to consider alternative fuel vehicles
items.summary_raw: Although developing non-fossil fuel vehicles supports sustainable urban transportation, their impact on air pollution and energy consumption depends on awareness of this technology. Aging fleets of Fossil Fuel Taxis (FFTs) cause environmental degradation, which replacing FFTs with Alternative Fuel Taxis (AFTs) mitigates. This study presents a novel framework investigating how personality and communication characteristics and taxi drivers’ knowledge of Alternative Fuel Vehicles (AFVs) shape awareness. It models awareness, persuasion, and willingness to purchase AFTs using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Based on 506 face-to-face Tehran taxi-driver interviews, PLS-SEM shows personality, communication characteristics, and AFV knowledge drive awareness with weights of 0.573, 0.627, and 0.168, respectively. Awareness affects persuasion, while persuasion strongly predicts willingness to purchase, explaining 51.4% of its variance; awareness explains 11.6% of persuasion variance. Pro-AFT policies providing ownership facilities and granting access permission to restricted city areas were examined as moderators, revealing differences across policy-support groups.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Net-Zero and Climate-Resilient Sustainable Cities: Technologies, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.summary_raw: Urbanization, climate change, increasing energy demand, and rapid infrastructure development have created significant challenges for achieving sustainable and resilient cities. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology that enables data-driven decision-making, intelligent automation, and efficient resource management, making it an important enabler of net-zero and climate-resilient urban systems. This narrative review examines AI applications relevant to urban climate mitigation and adaptation, drawing on literature identified through Google Scholar and ScienceDirect. The review examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, cloud computing, digital twins, and generative AI in improving urban energy systems, sustainable transportation, environmental monitoring, infrastructure management, and smart governance. The study also discusses how these technologies contribute to carbon emission reduction, renewable energy integration, climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and efficient urban planning. In addition, major challenges associated with AI implementation are critically analyzed, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, lack of interoperability, high energy consumption of AI systems, digital inequality, and governance issues. Emerging research trends such as explainable AI, green AI, AI-enabled digital twins, federated learning, and human-centered smart governance are…

items.title: Responsible agrivoltaics in temperate Europe: Making systems work for plants, people, and climate
items.summary_raw: Societal Impact Statement Agrivoltaics, the co‐location of solar panels and crops, is increasingly promoted to expand renewable energy without compromising agricultural areas. However, systems that are poorly designed impact productivity, landscape, and ecology, and face public criticism. Drawing on multi‐year, multi‐site field experience, this opinion paper discusses when and where agrivoltaics can deliver benefits and which trade‐offs are likely. We argue that responsible deployment requires clearer standards and evaluation frameworks that consider plant performance, soil integrity, and societal acceptance. By identifying recurring pitfalls, this work guides various stakeholders seeking to combine renewable energy generation with resilient food production while safeguarding rural landscapes. Summary Meeting climate neutrality goals requires more efficient land use for both food and renewable energy production. Agrivoltaics (AV) has emerged as a promising dual‐use strategy, but its optimal design and most appropriate implementation remain debated. Here, we synthesize insights from multiple years of four AV systems across Belgium, Denmark, and Germany to identify the conditions under which AV can deliver meaningful co‐benefits without compromising agricultural function. Across diverse crops and configurations, we highlight that temperate AV outcomes are governed by solar panel layout, interactions among microclimate modification, soil disturbance, water redistribution, and…

items.title: Life cycle carbon emission accounting and emission reduction potential assessment of container and domestic glass industry in China
items.summary_raw: The container and domestic glass (CDG) industry is one of the most energy-intensive sectors in China. To analyse the life cycle carbon emissions and the potential for carbon reduction of the CDG industry in China, we developed a carbon-emission accounting model based on life cycle assessment (LCA) and conducted an empirical analysis using 2023 as the baseline year. The study evaluates the carbon mitigation potential by adjusting four key variables: applying low-carbon technologies, optimising raw-material composition, modifying the fuel mix, and improving transportation methods. Sensitivity analysis was conducted to identify the critical factors influencing life cycle carbon emissions. Results indicate that the total life cycle CO2 emissions of the CDG industry in 2023 were estimated at 24.0 million tonnes, with raw material sourcing and manufacturing processes contributing over 98% of total emissions. Among all emission sources, fossil fuel consumption and raw material composition are identified as the primary targets for emission reduction. By 2030, the carbon reduction potential of the CDG industry is estimated at 22.85% through increased cullet use, 20.48% through adoption of energy-efficient and low-carbon technologies, 10.65% from optimising the fuel mix, and 0.61% through improvements in transportation methods. Fossil fuel combustion has the most significant impact on life cycle CO2 emissions, followed by changes in cullet usage and the carbon intensity of…

items.title: Kültürel ve politik faktörlerin sanatsal ifade özgürlüğüne etkileri
items.source_name: Uluslararası Sosyal Bilimler ve Eğitim Dergisi
items.summary_raw: Bu makalede, kültürel ve politik faktörlerin sanatsal ifade özgürlüğüne etkileri araştırılmıştır. Bu bağlamda araştırmada; Sovyetler Birliği ve Nazi Almanyası dönemlerinde sanatsal ifade özgürlüğüne yönelik engelleme girişimleri, Amerikan kültür savaşları, Sensation sergisi, Danimarka Muhammed karikatürleri ve AIDS salgını sürecinde sanatçılara yöneltilen suçlamalar ile sanatı sansürleme girişimleri incelenmiştir. Nitel araştırma yöntemlerinden literatür taranarak derlenen araştırmanın verileri; Dünya genelinde yankı uyandıran politik ve kültürel faktörler, dönemin sanatçıları ve sanat eserlerinden örnekler verilerek analiz edilmiştir. Sovyetler Birliği ve Nazi Almanya’sı zamanında sanatsal ifade özgürlüğünün devlet kontrolü altına alınması ve propaganda aracı haline getirilmesi, politik faktörlerin sanatsal ifade özgürlüğüne etkileri bakımından ekstrem örnekler olarak değerlendirilmiştir. Amerika Birleşik Devletleri’nde 1960 sonrasında başlayan ‘kültür savaşları’ döneminde, Robert Mapplethorpe ve Andres Serrano’nun eserlerine yönelik sansür girişimlerinin, gruplar arasında bir çeşit sosyal gerçekliği tanımlama mücadelesi olduğu gözlemlenmiştir. Bu bağlamda, kültürel ve politik dinamiklerin sanatsal ifade özgürlüğü üzerinde belirleyici bir rol oynadığı sonucuna varılmaktadır. Otoriter rejimlerde açık sansür ve kısıtlamalar öne çıkarken, liberal demokrasilerde kamuoyu baskısı, toplumsal normlar ve politik söylemler dolaylı sınırlayıcı etkiler yaratabilmektedir. items.title: From publication to action: connecting science, policy, and public attention for ocean-related climate mitigation
items.summary_raw: Ocean-related options (OROs), including marine renewable energy and ocean-based carbon dioxide removal, are emerging as promising climate mitigation actions. OROs vary widely in technological maturity and risk acceptability, yet as scientific literature exponentially increases, synthesising the current state of evidence is a major challenge. Using causal inference across diverse datasets from scientific publications, policy and legislation documents, social media posts, and deployment metrics, we identify scientific publications and social media attention as direct drivers of action. However, when social media attention overtakes research, actions may advance ahead of science – underscoring the need for responsive and robust policy development. Through a narrative analysis of three case studies, we identify that at a global scale, coordinated and well-designed policy with decisive implementation is key for catalysing step-changes in ORO progress. Together, our findings reveal the dynamic relationships linking science to action and highlight pathways for the effective and responsible scaling of OROs in the coming decades.

items.title: A multi-model analysis of hydrogen uptake in a climate-neutral Europe
items.summary_raw: Using an ensemble of integrated assessment models, we quantify the role of hydrogen in Europe’s energy transition under multiple climate policy scenarios. Hydrogen uptake in our net-zero scenario varies widely across models, ranging from 0.3 to 11.7 exajoules (average 4 exajoules) by 2050 and corresponding to 1-14% (average 7%) of final energy consumption, primarily in industry and synthetic fuel production. Hydrogen contributes minimally to electricity generation, and its direct use in transport and buildings remains limited. Despite projected carbon dioxide prices of 150–250 euros per tonne by 2030, hydrogen adoption remains below 2% (7 million tonnes) of final energy consumption, far below the European Union’s 2030 target of 20 million tonnes of green hydrogen from domestic production and imports. Hydrogen trade is scarcely modelled and therefore underrepresented. Our results support prioritizing near-term electrification while preparing strategically today for large-scale hydrogen expansion after 2040. Across multiple European energy models, deep decarbonization relies on strong early electrification, while hydrogen expands mainly after 2040 in hard-to-abate sectors; stronger policy support is essential for robust net-zero pathways.

items.title: Challenges and pathways for renewable energy transition amid crisis: A case study on community perspectives during the Russian war against Ukraine
items.summary_raw: The ongoing war in Ukraine has exposed the vulnerability of centralised energy systems while increasing the importance of decentralised renewable energy for maintaining essential public services. Existing research has largely focused on infrastructure damage, national energy policy, technological potential, and post-war reconstruction, with comparatively limited attention to how local governments make and implement energy decisions under conflict conditions. This study examines the extent to which Ukrainian territorial communities, or hromadas, can lead decentralised renewable energy transitions and identifies the institutional, financial, technical, and security-related conditions that shape this capacity. The analysis combines geospatial assessment of renewable-energy development with semi-structured interviews involving 19 hromadas across 10 oblasts, six complementary case studies, and a strategic assessment of enabling and constraining factors. The findings show substantial variation across security contexts. Hromadas located farther from the frontline and possessing stronger institutional capacity and donor connections are better positioned to deploy decentralised renewable energy, whereas frontline communities remain constrained by restricted access, infrastructure damage, investment risk, and limited technical capacity. Solar photovoltaic systems emerge as the most feasible community-level option, identified by approximately 90% of respondents, particularly for…

items.title: Midwives’ awareness of climate change and sustainability
items.summary_raw: This cross-sectional study examined climate-change awareness and sustainability consciousness among midwives and the association between the two scale scores. From September to October 2023, 100 midwives working in maternity units at two hospitals in southern Türkiye completed an online Demographic Information Form, the Climate Change Awareness Scale (CCAS), and the Sustainability Consciousness Questionnaire (SCQ). The CCAS covers awareness, problem perception, concern, and behaviours and policy expectations, whereas the SCQ covers sustainability knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours. Because these domains overlap, the total scores were interpreted as related multidimensional orientations rather than as distinct measures of awareness and knowledge. Participants had high mean CCAS and SCQ scores, and the total scores were positively correlated (r = .637, p < .001). CCAS scores differed by age group, and SCQ scores differed by educational level. These cross-sectional associations do not establish direction, mechanism, competence, or actual sustainable clinical practice. The findings identify an association between two partly overlapping constructs and show that media was the most frequently reported source of climate-change information. They support further investigation of climate literacy and education in midwifery, but should not be interpreted as evidence that awareness causes sustainable behaviour. The study is distinctive in examining the relationship between CCAS and SCQ…

items.title: High wind speed reduces water use efficiency across terrestrial ecosystems
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02781-z The role of wind in ecosystem water use efficiency remains unclear. The authors show that water use efficiency declines with increasing wind speed, driven mainly by increases in evapotranspiration and secondarily by reductions in gross primary productivity.

items.title: Beyond Victimhood: Gendering Climate Resilience in Indonesia through Feminist Participatory Action Research
items.summary_raw: This paper examines how gendered power relations shape climate resilience.Universalist approaches have predominantly framed climate change adaptation and resilience as technical issues, neglecting the deeply political and gendered dimensions of environmental decision-making.The discourse of victimhood that portrays women as vulnerable subjects in climate crisis narratives undermines women's agency, obscures the structural inequalities that limit their access to resources, and erases their leadership roles in grassroots climate adaptation.Using feminist participatory action research (FPAR) with three women's climate organisations in Kupang, Poso, and Yogyakarta, our paper moves beyond critiques of dominant approaches and towards the documentation of alternative lived practices of resilience and collective action in responding to environmental precarity.Our findings demonstrate that women-led groups employ diverse, contextually grounded adaptation approaches, reflecting localised resilience in diverse socioecological conditions.Despite varying intensities of climate impacts, from agrarian distress in rural areas to urban resource scarcity, gendered collective solidarity serves as a cohesive force in these initiatives, fostering innovative solutions such as community-based farming, disaster preparedness networks, and advocacy for policy reform.

items.title: Reconsidering pathways to global shipping decarbonization: idealism vs. realism
items.summary_raw: Introduction The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships and its 2025 Draft Net-Zero Framework exhibit evident features of idealism. These instruments have not fully considered vessels’ long-term asset cycles, technological bottlenecks for zero-carbon marine fuels, cross-country disparities in shipping development, and safety constraints related to green maritime infrastructure. Methods This study integrates legal realism, resource dependence theory, and securitization theory into a climate-realism framework. It uses doctrinal legal analysis, qualitative policy evaluation, and a Norway–China comparative case study. Results The limitations of the IMO Draft Net-Zero Framework are dissected across four dimensions: transition costs, technological maturity, carbon-pricing fairness, and infrastructure security. The Norway–China comparison shows that a one-size-fits-all aggressive pathway cannot reconcile industry survival with climate governance goals, whereas a gradual, inclusive, and technology-neutral route is more sustainable. Discussion To reconcile idealism with reality, global shipping decarbonization governance should establish a dynamic adjustment mechanism matched to technological iteration, implement differentiated carbon pricing, and build a transnational risk-sharing system for green infrastructure. This would balance development rights and maritime economic security while steadily promoting shipping decarbonization.

items.title: Warming oceans hit the battlefield
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02782-y Marine radar signal propagation is highly sensitive to fine-scale vertical changes in water vapour. Now research shows that long-term increases in sea surface temperatures are strengthening the frequency and intensity of the features that allow radar signals to travel further than expected.

items.title: The politics of calculative tools in practice: Climate budgeting in Edmonton
items.summary_raw: Climate budgeting aims to integrate carbon accounting into municipal financial budgeting, promising to align annual spending decisions with long-term emissions targets. Yet limited attention has been given to how this calculative framework operates within existing administrative practices and contested political contexts. This article examines the City of Edmonton’s 2022 Carbon Budget, the first municipal climate budget implemented in North America. Drawing on interviews, policy documents, and observations of public budget deliberations, it traces how carbon metrics were developed, applied to budget profiles, and interpreted by administrators and councillors. The analysis finds that efforts to translate climate impacts into conventional fiscal formats encountered substantial methodological limits. Most investments could not be quantified, indirect and longer-term effects remained excluded, and aggregated results suggested proposed climate investments would have little effect on Edmonton’s emissions pathway. Rather than increasing transparency or building consensus, the project intensified disagreements over municipal responsibilities, public support, and the justification of climate spending. Comparison with Oslo demonstrates that climate budgeting’s effects may depend less on technical design than on the political authority, administrative capacity, and institutional relationships within which it operates. Climate budgeting should be understood not as a transferable…

items.title: The Use of Styrofoam as an Innovative Building Component in Calabar, Cross River State: Implications for Sustainable Architectural Practice
items.summary_raw: The persistent housing deficit, indoor thermal discomfort, and rising energy demand in Nigeria’s humid-tropical climate have triggered a search for innovative building components that advance energy efficiency and sustainability in the construction industry. In Calabar, Cross River State, where rapid urbanization and informal construction patterns coexist with climatic vulnerability, the adoption of expanded polystyrene (EPS), commonly known as Styrofoam, as an architectural component remains under-explored, particularly in walling, insulation, and prefabricated systems. This paper evaluates the thermal performance, construction efficiency, cost implications, durability, fire safety, and user acceptance of EPS; analyses its architectural applications in walling, roofing insulation, ceilings, partitions, and lightweight prefabricated systems in Calabar; and examines its physical, thermal, acoustic, structural, and environmental properties. A qualitative, descriptive research approach is adopted, combining an extensive literature review (2018–2026) with field observations, photographic documentation, and multi-site case studies of EPS-based buildings in Nigeria, Africa, Europe, Asia, and North America. Empirical evidence from EPS-panel projects and EPS-crete-type composites suggests that Styrofoam can function effectively as insulation, fascias, cornices, and non-structural elements, but must be integrated within appropriate building codes, detailing, and fire-protection…

items.title: It depends on the question: How survey format shapes the measurement of public attitudes to carbon capture and storage in Norway
items.summary_raw: Public attitudes towards emerging, technically complex climate technologies are difficult to measure with standard closed-ended items. When an issue is unfamiliar and low in salience, closed formats may invite low-effort, weakly held answers that mask uncertainty and ambivalence. We examine how question format shapes the measurement of public support for carbon capture and storage, using a probability-based online survey of the Norwegian public fielded in 2020 ( n = 3068). Respondents read a brief information text, wrote an open-ended response, then answered a closed forced-choice item. The two formats yield different pictures of opinion. In their own words, 26% of respondents gave unqualified support and 30% supported the technology only conditionally; the combined positive share was 56%, against 66% in the closed item. ‘No opinion’ was selected by 23% in the closed item but appeared in only 4% of the open-ended responses, whereas non-response was higher for the open question (14% vs. 0.4%). Among respondents selecting ‘No opinion’ in the closed item, around 60% expressed a substantive evaluation in open text, often ambivalent, conditional or negative. Respondents whose open text was not positive but who nonetheless chose ‘Positive’ wrote longer, not shorter, responses. Environmental impacts, leakage, safety, costs and efficacy dominate the reservations expressed. These patterns point to a measurement trade-off: closed items are efficient but may overstate support and…

items.title: Net carbon emission accounts, drivers, and mitigation measures in China, 1980–2020
items.summary_raw: Mitigating net CO 2 emissions under socioeconomic development and climate variability is essential for climate action and sustainable development goals. Here, focusing on anthropogenic emissions and terrestrial ecosystem sinks, we construct a national-scale account of China's net emissions from 1980 to 2020, examine their evolution, and quantify the contributions of drivers and mitigation measures. We found that anthropogenic emissions dominated the long-term increase in net emissions, while ecosystem sinks offset only ∼12–32% of the increase in anthropogenic emissions. Meanwhile, the sensitivity of ecosystem sinks to climate variability introduced interannual fluctuations in net emissions, especially through responses to irradiance and precipitation anomalies. By combining an extended Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index decomposition with scenario simulations of ecosystem sinks, we found that rising affluence was the main driver of increasing net emissions, whereas declining energy intensity was the main mitigation measure. Land-use management and vegetation-related sink efficiency generally reduced net emissions, but their contributions weakened over time. The direct climate-related effect on ecosystem sinks differed across periods and was comparable to some anthropogenic drivers. By linking anthropogenic emissions, ecosystem sinks, and climate variability over four decades, this study provides a basis for assessing net-zero pathways under socioeconomic development and climate…

items.title: Climate Change in the State Executive Agenda
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT State of the state (SOTS) speeches represent an annual opportunity for governors to identify issues they intend to prioritize in the coming year. The speeches represent a finite agenda space directed at lawmakers as well as the general public. In this paper, we use SOTS speeches to assess the attention American governors directed toward climate change from 2020 to 2024. Climate change is a particularly useful topic to explore substantively because of the outsized role states play in climate policy in the United States. We address three research questions. (1) What role does gubernatorial party have in determining the agenda presence of climate change? (2) What is the influence of legislative control versus divided government on climate agenda presence? (3) To what extent is climate change associated with other issues in SOTS speeches? Our dataset contains 60,801 manually coded quasi‐sentences from 235 speeches. We find that Democrats mention climate change more than Republicans, that this difference is greatest between government trifectas, but that Democratic and Republican governors speaking to divided legislatures shape their message to meet the partisan split. We also find that climate change is associated with a host of other issues, but that Democratic governors associate climate change with a broader range of issues than Republicans. Our work contributes to gubernatorial politics, climate politics, and agenda‐setting scholarship.

items.title: The limits of critical thinking: climate skepticism, epistemic trespassing, and the understanding that grounds trust
items.source_name: European Journal for Philosophy of Science
items.summary_raw: Abstract What should the public understand about climate change to form true beliefs and responsibly participate in democratic deliberation? We argue for a partly negative and partly positive answer. Negatively, the public does not need to understand the climate or first-order evidence in climate science: endeavors that pursue such first-order competence, such as mainstream critical thinking (CT) and logic-based inoculation strategies task non-experts with a demand they cannot reliably perform. We demonstrate this by applying such inoculation procedures to a sophisticated and credentialed argument against climate change, and show that encouraging non-experts to evaluate the first-order premises and scientific claims leads to epistemic trespassing. Positively, we argue that what the public actually needs for responsible participation in the climate debate is a more modest and attainable understanding of the social epistemology of science – understanding how the scientific consensus is formed and why the process is more reliable than the alternatives. This kind of understanding transforms blind reliance into rationally warranted trust. In doing so, we distinguish the process of higher-order critical assessment, the understanding it gives, and the calibrated deference it licenses, and we locate higher-order evidence on the side of warranted trust rather than first-order understanding. The result is an epistemically responsible framework for public engagement with climate…

items.title: Political affiliation and extreme weather effects on climate information search and decisions [ Registered Report Stage 1 Protocol]
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACTIncreasing political polarization may not only endanger efforts to reduce carbon emissions but also shape how the public responds to intensifying extreme weather events caused by climate change. While previous research has examined the impact of political affiliation on (un)sustainable decisions, little is known about how it shapes underlying psychological processes such as climate-relevant information search in contexts with high or low extreme weather exposure. This study investigates how political affiliation and extreme weather exposure influence information search processes in a decision-making task with real-world climate consequences in a representative U.S. sample (N = 2,000). We hypothesize that Democrats will prioritize climate-related information more than Republicans, with this effect amplified by recent extreme weather exposure, especially when events are attributed to climate change. Our findings could inform targeted group-specific communication, eventspecific messaging, and how attention to climate change may evolve in response to intensifying political divides and extreme weather events. items.title: Combining climate policy instruments for a just transition to a climate-neutral economy
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02757-z A distributional analysis of European Union climate policy pathways traces the costs of reducing carbon dioxide emissions to the level of households based on their spending and income patterns. We find that different equity considerations, including income inequality and within-group impact divergence, can shape optimal climate policy design with carbon prices, transfers, standards and subsidies.

items.title: So Close, but Different: Uncovering the Different Determinants of Eco-Innovation in Central Europe
items.summary_raw: Central European countries face lower environmental awareness, reflected in the limited number of studies on eco-innovation in this area. This study contributes to research on environmental innovation in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, which have been among the major European polluters in the past. In contrast to previous studies, we focus on indicators such as energy management, waste minimisation and recycling, and air pollution control measures. The results show that despite the geographical and historical proximity of the Czech Republic and Slovakia, environmental innovation is influenced by different determinants in different areas. In the Czech Republic, the presence of a manager responsible for the environment and climate change was confirmed as a key determinant of firms’ environmental initiatives. In Czech and Slovak firms, environmental regulations trigger environmental innovation, specifically those measures focused on reducing emissions, directly impacting public health and environmental protection. At the same time the Environmental and CO2 Emission goals are an incentive for eco-innovation in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. This paper serves several practical implications, both for policymakers and practitioners. First, we suggest introducing tax incentives or low-interest loan programmes that could encourage businesses to invest in renewable energy and improve energy efficiency within analysed countries. items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Sustainability and Climate Change Mitigation: Recent Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Abstract Climate change and environmental degradation have emerged as two of the most pressing global challenges of the twenty-first century, threatening ecosystems, biodiversity, human health, and sustainable development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed environmental research and management by enabling advanced data analytics, real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and intelligent decision-support systems. This review critically examines the applications of AI in addressing environmental and climate-related challenges, including climate forecasting, air and water quality monitoring, biodiversity conservation, precision agriculture, renewable energy optimization, carbon emission assessment, waste management, and disaster risk reduction. Furthermore, The review also identifies current research gaps and highlights future opportunities for developing transparent, energy-efficient, and explainable AI systems that support evidence-based environmental decisionmaking. It concludes that AI has become a transformative tool for accelerating progress toward climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability, and the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, and policy support will be essential to maximize the environmental benefits of AI while minimizing its ecological footprint. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Climate Change; Environmental Sustainability…

items.title: Warming-driven lower-tropospheric stratification intensifies ducting over global oceans
items.summary_raw: Under global warming, the marine atmospheric boundary layer shows an increase in lower-tropospheric stratification. These thermodynamic shifts alter vertical refractivity gradients and can modulate atmospheric ducts, which are natural waveguides crucial for beyond-line-of-sight electromagnetic propagation. Using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1940 to 2025, we find a global-scale intensification of atmospheric ducts over oceans at mid- to low-latitude, with a robust increasing trend in atmospheric duct occurrence probability, strength and top height. Mechanistically, this intensification is intrinsically coupled with the sustained increase in static stability in the marine atmospheric boundary layer. Although interannual climate modes, such as the El Niño/Southern Oscillation, modulate these anomalies, the long-term warming trend dominates the long-term trend. Ultimately, continuous warming is shifting the marine atmospheric background state towards a highly stratified regime favouring more frequent and intense ducting, with implications for global maritime communication, radar and navigation systems. Atmospheric ducts are waveguides that affect electromagnetic propagation in the atmosphere, affecting radar and other technologies. Here the authors show that warming intensifies such ducting over mid- to low-latitude oceans.

items.title: Integrating agenda-setting theory and the health belief model to understand newspaper coverage of postpartum depression and maternal help-seeking behaviour in Nigeria
items.source_name: Aminu Kano Academic Scholars Association Multidisciplinary Journal
items.summary_raw: Despite being a major but poorly recognised mental health condition among women in Nigeria, postpartum depression (PPD) is still neglected due to cultural stigma, lack of mental health literacy and lack of media coverage. Current studies have investigated the portrayal of PPD in the media and mental health stigma alone, and have not explained how the media coverage turns into individual beliefs that stimulate or hinder help-seeking. This theoretical essay fills that gap by examining the synergy between agenda-setting theory (AST) and health belief model (HBM) to illustrate the public salience of PPD as generated by newspaper coverage indicators, frequency of coverage, prominence, framing, priming, and depth, and the filtering of public salience through perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy to shape maternal responses. Writes the article, the continued coverage of PPD in a culturally responsive manner in newspapers can move this from a private, spiritual issue to a legitimate public health issue, while stigmatising or superficial coverage can cause silence to reign. Discussion about implications for health communication practice, journalistic training and maternal mental health policy in low- and middle-income contexts is discussed.

As climate change reshapes the contexts of practice, counselor educators must prepare students for climate-informed advocacy. This manuscript positions the ACES Climate Change and Environmental Justice Competencies as an operational framework for advocacy identity development. Through a narrative case mapped across CACREP domains, we illustrate implications for program design, mentorship, research, and leadership preparation.

items.title: Beyond Harmony: Climate Adaptation, Gender Inequality, and Symbolic Governance in Bali
items.summary_raw: This study critically examines the celebrated Balinese subak irrigation system.The subak is an irrigation group for water control and allocation over a regional area, traditionally guided by the Tri Hita Karana (THK) philosophy of harmony.We argue that this idealised narrative obscures structural inequalities and gendered exclusion embedded within subak governance, particularly as communities face intensifying climate stressors.Investigating two sites-Jatiluwih (rural, high tourism) and Margaya (peri-urban)-through intersectional analysis, utilising Participatory Focus Group Discussions and interviews we explore how women's labour and agency are shaped by spatial governance and symbolic discourses.Women's exclusion from decision-making stems from a systemic rationalisation of hierarchy as essential for morality order.This creates a governance blind spot: climate adaptation interventions, designed as gender-neutral, yield profoundly biased outcomes, reinforcing existing inequalities and hindering equitable adaptation for smallholder farmers.

items.title: How does energy transition in China amidst climate risk shocks influence residents’ welfare?
items.summary_raw: China regards energy transition as a significant measure to handle global climate change and foster the harmonious coexistence of human beings and nature. This article matches the urban energy transition index with China Family Panel Studies data to systematically examine and evaluate the impact of energy transition on residents’ happiness. The baseline results indicate that energy transition has improved residents’ happiness. Mechanism analysis found that energy transition did not significantly change residents’ inherent energy consumption habits, while reducing their perception of wealth gap and increasing their favorability towards the government. Heterogeneity results indicate that the positive impact of energy transition on residents’ happiness is more prominent in rural, coastal, and middle-aged and elderly populations. In addition, climate policy uncertainty and climate physical risks incentivize residents to achieve higher levels of happiness during the energy transition process. This article is of great significance for the rational arrangement of China’s energy transition process as well as achieving a win-win situation between energy transition and residents’ happiness.

items.title: From perception to policy assessment: revealing socio-demographic biases in environmental decision-making
items.summary_raw: Climate policies are typically designed based on technical, economic, and institutional considerations. This study looks at how different social backgrounds shape the way people rank environmental priorities. Based on survey data from over 1500 people across Europe, we examine how gender, income, education, political beliefs, job roles, and regional identity influence these choices. We also revisit the WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) bias, originally used to critique psychology research, and explore how similar dynamics affect European environmental policy assessments. Our findings reveal that women, lower-income groups, and left-leaning respondents prioritize fairness and basic needs, while experts and wealthier individuals tend to focus on technical and long-term issues. These patterns suggest that policy decisions are never socially neutral and making environmental strategies more inclusive means recognizing these biases and designing processes that reflect the full diversity of public values.

items.title: An Unexpected Beneficiary of the Permitting Bill: Mini Marine Power
items.summary_raw: Tucked inside the Senate’s ambitious new permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is a major win for an energy technology that often flies under the radar: marine power. Small-scale wave, tidal, and river-current projects could help power everything from remote communities and military installations to ocean sensors and coastal desalination systems — at least in theory. Drawing largely from the bipartisan FLOWS Act , introduced in the Senate last December but never brought to a floor vote, BAAJA aims to streamline the licensing pathway for so-called micro hydrokinetic projects, which harness moving water without dams or reservoirs and have a capacity of 5 megawatts or less. The bill would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission one year to act on commercial license applications for these projects, while exempting them from full review under the National Environmental Policy Act. It would also allow FERC to issue 10- to 20-year licenses, giving projects a pathway to long-term commercial operation, as opposed to relying on pilot licenses designed for temporary testing. The bill wouldn’t eliminate environmental oversight altogether. Small-scale marine energy projects would still undergo basic environmental screenings as a part of FERC licensing, and would still require state and local permits, which can trigger their own environmental reviews. items.title: Convergent genome streamlining accompanies independent miniaturization in the world’s smallest fishes
items.summary_raw: Miniaturization, the reduction of adult body size to an extreme degree, has evolved repeatedly across vertebrates. Yet its genomic underpinnings remain poorly understood. Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater fishes, contains multiple miniaturized lineages that have evolved via contrasting developmental processes. Proportioned dwarfs are tiny-bodied but otherwise morphologically similar to larger relatives, while progenetic miniatures exhibit developmental truncation and retain larval-like anatomical features into adulthood. Using a new time-calibrated phylogeny of 309 cypriniform species and comparative genomic analyses of 33 high-quality genome assemblies, we investigated the evolutionary history and genomic correlates of miniaturization across this order. Ancestral state reconstruction revealed multiple independent origins of both miniature types, with reversals to the nonminiature state rarely recovered and miniature origins nonrandomly distributed across the phylogeny. The origins of the two types of miniatures differed in their timing. Progenetic miniatures arose predominantly in the Eocene whereas proportioned dwarfs arose mainly within the Miocene period. Genome size variation across Cypriniformes has been overwhelmingly driven by polyploidy. However, progenetic miniatures showed a directionally consistent, though nonsignificant, trend toward genome size reduction. items.title: Shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves through promoting CsMYB7-like-mediated conversion of Se (VI) to Se (IV)
items.summary_raw: Limited selenium (Se) accumulation in agricultural products contributes to widespread dietary Se deficiency, posing a global nutritional threat. Efficient agronomic strategies to enhance Se biofortification in crops are still lacking. Here, we reveal the synergistic effects of shading and Se nanoparticles application on Se biofortification in tea leaves. Field experiments demonstrate that shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves under sufficient Se supply, through activating Se metabolism pathway. We identify CsAPR1 functions at the early stage of Se assimilation, catalyzing the reduction of Se (VI). The transcription of CsAPR1 is activated by CsMYB7-like and is further promoted by shading through interaction with CsbHLH70. Under sunlight, CsHY5 competes with CsbHLH70 for binding to CsMYB7-like, thereby attenuating CsMYB7-like-mediated transcription of CsAPR1 and suppressing Se accumulation in tea plants. Our findings reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying shade-induced enhancement of Se biofortification, offering insights and strategies for Se-enriched crop production.

items.title: Ice-ray pentagonal packing of pseudo-fivefold helices
items.summary_raw: While fivefold point symmetry is common in nature, fivefold spatial symmetry is seldom observed. Regular pentagons cannot tile a plane without leaving voids, and even the densest “ice-ray” packing is exceptionally rare. Fivefold helices are equally elusive. We report a small molecule that self-assembles into hydrogen-bonded pseudo-fivefold helices and adopts an ice-ray pentagonal packing motif over crystallographic length scales using peripheral disorder that partially occupies regions that would otherwise be void in an ideal pentagonal tessellation. The resulting structure exhibits weak and nondirectional interhelical interactions within the ( bc ) plane and comparatively strong and directional intrahelical hydrogen bonding along the a axis. This structural anisotropy gives rise to single crystals with large aspect ratios and distinct mechanical behavior. This realization of two rare structural motifs within a single crystal shows the capability of simple organic molecules to form complex structures and highlights an untapped potential for symmetry engineering in molecular solids through the interplay of intermolecular interactions with pronounced differences in strength and directionality.

items.title: Autoimmunity induced by epigenome alteration affecting thymic Treg cell development
items.summary_raw: Methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 3 (MBD3), an essential component of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, controls chromatin accessibility at lineage-specific transcriptional enhancers and promoters during hematopoietic cell differentiation. Here, we have shown that MBD3 deficiency in the T cell compartment resulted in spontaneous development of T cell–mediated multiorgan autoimmune diseases including fatal autoimmune myocarditis. The MBD3-deficient mice notably showed a significant reduction of CD25 + Foxp3 + regulatory T (Treg) cells in both the thymus and periphery without much affecting the development and function of conventional T (Tconv) cells. Mixed bone marrow (BM) chimeras reconstituted with wild-type and MBD3-deficient BM revealed a cell-intrinsic defect in thymic Treg cell lineage differentiation in MBD3-deficient cells. Transcriptional, phenotypic, and functional analyses of thymocyte subsets further revealed that MBD3 deficiency particularly affected the activation of a Treg-specific enhancer of the Il2ra gene encoding CD25, hence impaired CD25 expression in immature CD4 single-positive thymocytes (ImCD4SP) but not in peripheral T cells. The impairment markedly limited thymic Treg precursor cell generation and substantially reduced overall thymic Treg cell output. items.title: After a decade of wildfires, an overlooked election could shape California’s climate future
items.summary_raw: Insurance is a social contract. When you sign up with State Farm or Allstate for home insurance, you confirm your membership in a community — your money will go to fix someone else’s burned or flooded home, and their money will in turn support yours. We let insurance companies sell policies on a private market, and we elect or appoint government officials to oversee that market to protect the interests of homeowners. That’s how it’s supposed to work, but that’s not how it panned out for Lynn McIntyre. When McIntyre’s mother died in 2022, she willed McIntyre her longtime house in the “Alphabets,” a charming neighborhood not far from the coast in western Los Angeles. McIntyre and her daughter had only lived there for a year when her insurance company, Liberty Mutual, withdrew her fire coverage. She couldn’t find another private company to cover the home’s fire risk, so she enrolled in the California FAIR Plan, a state-backed “insurer of last resort,” paying another $5,000 a year in addition to her regular home insurance from Liberty. After the Palisades Fire raged through the Alphabets in early 2025, McIntyre’s small bungalow was still standing. But it was full of smoke and ash that had crept in through vents and windows, and her belongings were stained beyond recognition by smoke. When she filed a claim with the FAIR Plan, the plan adjusters told her she was out of luck. They would pay for a temporary apartment, but nothing else. McIntyre, who had worked for years as a real…

items.title: Pampered city trees deal with stress better than their country cousins
items.summary_raw: The next time you pass an urban tree, stop to appreciate what it’s been through. As a youngster, it was especially vulnerable to pests and diseases, not to mention vandalism. Now grown up, it must contend with ever-rising temperatures due to the heat island effect — the built environment’s tendency to soak up solar energy and slowly release it at night. You might assume, then, that city trees are by default worse off than their rural counterparts. But new research suggests that urban vegetation is more resilient than you might think. Using satellite data from 2001 to 2022, researchers found that in more than three-quarters of 751 cities worldwide, plant life better coped with climate stresses like extreme heat than greenery in the surrounding countryside. In one-third of those municipalities, trees showed a “dual advantage,” losing less greenness from pressures in the first place, but also recovering faster from them. That’s allowing metropolitan vegetation to do what it does best: reduce temperatures by providing shade, boost biodiversity by creating habitats, and mitigate flooding by allowing rainwater to soak into soil instead of pooling on concrete. “Generally, the urban environment is harsher for vegetation — for example, the air temperature and also the air pollution,” said Zhengfei Guo, an ecologist at the University of Hong Kong and lead author of a new paper describing the research. “Therefore, our results that found urban vegetation is more resilient than rural…

items.title: The vital role of ponds for biodiversity, climate, and people
Shifting balance between habitat and climate in boreal biodiversity patterns across space, time and taxa
items.summary_raw: Climate and habitat are key drivers of biodiversity patterns. However, how they independently and jointly affect species distribution across space, time, and taxa remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluate the relative importance of habitat and climate variables underpinning occurrence and abundance patterns of 503 terrestrial animal species over 20 years and a ~ 1100 km latitudinal gradient in Finland. Habitat composition is the main explanatory variable of biodiversity patterns, with varying importance and uncertainty across taxa, regions, and years, and with effects being partially correlated for many species. Specifically, habitat dominate in importance for butterflies, birds, and small mammals, while both habitat and climate explain the patterns of large mammals and moths. Additionally, patterns between biogeographical regions and years are mainly explained by climate, while habitat explains most variation within regions and years. Further differences emerge among functional groups, as body size, pace of life and specialization modulate the relative importance of habitat and climate. Our findings emphasize that land use is a major force in shaping terrestrial biodiversity, while highlighting its tight connection with climate. Considering functional, spatial, and temporal contexts is thus essential for building effective conservation strategies for biodiversity under global change. Climate and habitat jointly shape species distributions and biodiversity. The authors…

items.title: Architects as educators in owner-occupied retrofit: Situated learning in design interactions
items.summary_raw: Retrofitting owner-occupied housing is critical to achieving decarbonisation targets, yet uptake remains limited. While social approaches emphasise building experts' role in engaging households with retrofit, the interactional agency of architects remains insufficiently specified within energy research. This study examines how architects can enable owner-occupiers to engage with low-carbon retrofit within wider home improvement projects. A micro-ethnographic study combined six observations of early design interactions with fifteen in-depth interviews with architects and owner-occupiers in England and Wales. Participating architects worked in purposively selected micro-practices committed to low-carbon design. Drawing on practice theory, the study conceptualised retrofit as emerging within a nexus of practices. It introduced learning pathways to trace how competences developed through design interactions connect with meanings, material arrangements and further competences in owner-occupiers' practices. These pathways informed reflexive thematic analysis. The most prominent pathway concerned the reconfiguration of worth, consisting of jointly reconsidering what constituted worthwhile improvements within particular projects, especially where retrofit was not initially planned. Developing retrofit competences and managing material risks supported this process, helping owner-occupiers evaluate low-carbon options in relation to their aspirations and existing homes. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Off-Grid Renewable Energy Systems in Nigeria
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize off-grid renewable energy systems in Nigeria by enhancing efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. This study employs a qualitative research approach using secondary data sources to examine the role of AI-driven technologies in optimizing energy generation, distribution, and storage. Anchored in the Technological Innovation System (TIS) theory, the research explores how AI innovations can transform decentralized energy networks while identifying barriers to adoption. Findings indicate that AIpowered predictive analytics enhance energy demand forecasting, reducing inefficiencies and minimizing waste. AI-driven smart grids improve real-time power distribution, and battery management systems optimize storage performance, extending battery lifespan. However, key challenges—including high implementation costs, limited data infrastructure, technical skills shortages, and regulatory constraints—hinder AI adoption in Nigeria’ s energy sector. Case studies from India and Kenya illustrate successful AI applications in off-grid electrification, offering valuable lessons for Nigeria. To facilitate AI integration, policy interventions, publicprivate partnerships, capacity-building initiatives, and improved digital infrastructure are recommended. By leveraging AI innovations, Nigeria can advance rural electrification, promote sustainable energy access, and drive economic development.

items.title: Media-based reflections to foster climate literacy in mathematics teacher education
items.summary_raw: Abstract In teacher education, there is an urgent need to prepare graduates with the knowledge, skills and ethical dispositions required to address pressing global challenges, particularly climate change. This study was conducted in a mathematics teacher education programme at a public university in Hong Kong, where undergraduate prospective teachers (PTs) in mathematics engaged in media-based learning activities involving structured reflection and dialogue on pedagogical approaches for integrating climate literacy into mathematics teaching. Drawing on discourse analysis of PTs’ written reflections and group discussions, the study examines how they made sense of the climate emergency and their professional responsibilities as future educators. The findings indicate that media-based reflections fostered shared attention, emotional engagement, and a sense of collective responsibility among PTs. Participants also articulated shifts in perspective and envisaged changes to their mathematics teaching practices across three thematic areas: (1) raising awareness of climate change via cultivating data literacy, (2) teaching environmental sustainability through mathematical modelling, and (3) fostering critical evaluation of quantitative information and representations. This study highlights how media-based reflective pedagogies in mathematics teacher education can support the development of climate literacy by strengthening PTs’ capacity for critical reflection on sustainability…

items.title: From Intention to Practice: How Collective Teacher Efficacy and Inclusive School Climate Shape Inclusive Teaching Practices in China
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Teachers play a crucial role in achieving high‐quality inclusive education, highlighting the need to understand the belief‐related factors that influence their intentions and practices. Drawing on Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour, this study examined how teachers' perceptions of collective teacher efficacy and an inclusive school climate are associated with teachers' attitudes, self‐efficacy, intentions to teach inclusively, and their inclusive teaching practices. Using cross‐sectional survey data from 1418 Chinese teachers, structural equation modelling showed that perceived collective teacher efficacy and an inclusive school climate were significantly associated with attitudes and self‐efficacy, which, in turn, related to intentions; these intentions strongly correlated with inclusive teaching practices. Multi‐group analyses revealed that leadership role, professional background, and gender moderated several key pathways. The findings underscore the value of cultivating teachers' perceptions of collective capability and an inclusive school climate, as well as tailoring professional development to different teacher groups.

items.title: Climate Disaster Exposure, Eco-Anxiety, and Hope Among Pakistani Youth: Agency and Trust as Moderators
items.summary_raw: Climate change is increasingly recognized as a psychological as well as environmental challenge, and the vulnerability of the younger generation in Pakistan due to the adverse effects of climate change is of particular concern. This study examined the relationship between distress associated with exposure to climate disasters, climate-change hope, and Eco-anxiety among Pakistani youth and the moderating role of political trust and perceived agency. A cross-A sectional, correlational survey design was used, and data were collected from 255 young adults aged 18-29 from educational institutions and social media. Participants filled out validated scale measures on levels of disaster-related distress, political trust, sense of agency, eco-anxiety, and climate change hope. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS v.25. Model results revealed that disaster distress was a significant positive predictor of eco-anxiety, but not climate change hope. Additionally, none of the hypothesized moderations were supported by the results, pointing to alternative mechanisms of the development of eco-anxiety, as well as climate change hope among the sample. The study may help to inform interventions towards building youth agency, enhancing communication of trauma-informed messages, and enhancing institutional trust.

items.title: The ambitions and limitations of climate assemblies
Fueling resentment: From vulnerability to fuel price increases to political discontent
items.summary_raw: Vulnerability to fuel price increases in the transport sector arises from high car use, low income and car dependence (i.e., poor accessibility by alternative modes). This issue is of increasing relevance due to climate policy (e.g., ETS-2 in the EU) and geopolitical conflicts pushing fuel prices up, as well as concerns that this might result in political discontent. While previous research has shown that this vulnerability is geographically uneven, its relationships with infrastructure provision, other forms of socio-economic vulnerability and voting patterns remain unclear. We fill this gap by bringing together research on transport energy vulnerability, the “foundational economy” and political discontent in an empirical study of 1,180 municipalities in Piedmont (Italy). We build a composite index of Vulnerability to Fuel Price Increases and compare it with broader socio-economic vulnerability metrics, a Foundational Economy Index measuring foundational services, and with voting patterns in Italian general elections. Crossing fuel and socio-economic vulnerability reveals four municipal typologies; municipalities vulnerable in at least one dimension comprise 734 municipalities and over 730,000 residents. These profiles vary across conventional classifications and foundational economy provision and therefore would risk being overlooked by redistributive interventions unless bespoke indicators are used. items.title: Citizens’ assemblies propose ambitious climate policy but impacts remain limited
items.summary_raw: Abstract Climate citizens’ assemblies convene randomly selected citizens who, after structured learning and deliberation, develop policy recommendations. Yet, whether they produce more ambitious recommendations and influence political decisions remains contested. Here we conduct a comparative, counterfactual assessment of 488 recommendations from five national and one state-level assembly in Western Europe, drawing on document analysis and expert interviews. The results show that citizens consistently proposed more ambitious climate measures than existing government policy. Recommendations sometimes influenced policy by adding momentum, enriching plans, breaking deadlocks or introducing novel ideas, but such influence was rare. Only the French assembly shows substantial policy impact, with one-third of its recommendations having influenced policy, due to strong power delegation, political leadership and resulting public pressure. In the other cases, policy impact was minimal or absent. These findings show that citizens’ assemblies can raise policy ambition, but translating recommendations into political decisions depends strongly on political conditions.

items.title: From Awareness to Action: Assessing Changes in Climate Change Perceptions and Active Citizenship among Students after an educational intervention
items.summary_raw: This study examined the effects of an educational intervention on senior high school Greek students’ perceptions of climate change, motivation for active citizenship and volunteering, and sense of individual and collective responsibility in crisis management. A repeated-measures design was employed, with participants (N = 29 before; N = 25 after) completing validated self-report scales before and after the intervention. Results indicated a modest overall improvement in mean scores across all variables following the intervention. Significant correlations among the three domains were observed both pre- and post-intervention, but with stronger associations after the intervention. Cluster analysis revealed three participant response profiles indicating heterogeneous intervention effects. The findings highlight the nuanced nature of students’ cognitive engagement with climate change and civic responsibility, underscoring the potential of targeted educational interventions to foster sustainable, pro-social attitudes.

items.title: Love Without Borders: Explaining Why People Interact with National Out-Groups on Tinder
items.summary_raw: Despite our tendency to select romantic partners who are similar to us, a growing body of research seems to suggest that online dating may increase the diversity of couples. However, to this day, there is no clarity around what might drive users to cross social boundaries on these platforms. Building on the Theory of Reasoned Action, we propose a model that integrates individual (e.g. attitudes, perceived norms), relational (e.g. intergroup contact, social identity), and platform-specific antecedents (e.g. use motivation, experience) that could explain national-identity-based intergroup interactions on Tinder. Based on a survey with 668 adult Tinder users living in the Netherlands and the UK, recruited through an online panel, we found that norms and attitudes both positively related to intentions to date national out-groups, which was in turn associated with behavior. Intergroup contact positively relates to intergroup dating norms and, in turn, intergroup dating intentions. The strength of social identity and different motives for using Tinder did not influence intentions. Frequent Tinder usage was linked to greater out-group dating intentions, suggesting online dating could lead to more diverse relationships regarding nationality. Findings highlight the role of intergroup contact and social norms in digital romantic settings.

items.title: A new place for stories in conservation
items.summary_raw: Michael Soule writes in his foundational article "What is Conservation Biology?" that "in crisis disciplines, one must act before knowing all the facts; crisis disciplines are thus a mixture of science and art, and their pursuit requires intuition as well as information." Since this article was published three decades ago, conservation biology has largely focused its energies on formalizing and memorializing its scientific findings. There is no doubt this empirical turn has developed vital methods and tools, enabled links between science and policy, and fortified the discipline's credibility within the broader biological sciences. Nevertheless, Soule's intuition that conservation biology requires a kinship with art, and particularly with storytelling, remains essential to the discipline-particularly in an information environment saturated by generative artificial intelligence-in at least three important ways. First, as a crisis discipline, conservation biology remains firmly attached to questions of not only valuation but also value, which have always relied on stories and myth for expression and enrichment. Second, conservationists continue to find that stories are at least as effective as logic in communicating results and precipitating action. Fortunately, conservation science lends itself to narrative arcs by demonstrating evidence of change. Revelations of the degradation and restoration of biological diversity rhyme with myths of loss and redemption and create…

items.title: Where Commitment Dissipates: An Attenuation Cascade Theory of Gender in Climate Resilience Policy
items.summary_raw: Climate policy increasingly recognises that unequal social relations shape climate risk, yet this recognition has not consistently changed budgets, eligibility rules, or outcomes. This article examines where near-universal gender commitments weaken and what determines the scale of that loss. Using theory-building thematic synthesis, it integrates feminist political ecology, intersectionality, social vulnerability theory, the capabilities approach, and transformative resilience with research on policy evaporation and gradual institutional change. It develops attenuation cascade theory, which proposes that gender commitments carry integration depth through six institutional conversions: framing, mandate, budget, eligibility, distribution, and outcome. Transmission is multiplicative, making realised depth dependent on the weakest conversion rather than the initial strength of commitment. Five propositions address the ordering of integration across analytical domains, concentration of loss at two critical conversions, distributive selectivity of formally neutral rules, differential survivability of policy instruments, and the role of independent verification in detecting attenuation. Evidence shows that gender is referenced in 95.0 per cent of national adaptation plans and by 81.5 per cent of Parties in their latest nationally determined contributions, yet fewer than one third of assessed contributions provide comprehensive treatment. Only 0.04 to about 3 per cent of…

items.title: The Impact of Solar Energy Expansion on Rural Electrification in Africa
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: Energy poverty remains a critical barrier to socioeconomic development in rural Africa, where millions lack access to reliable electricity. This study explores the state of rural electrification, the consequences of dependence on traditional energy sources, and the potential of solar energy as a viable solution. Using a qualitative secondary research methodology, the study synthesizes data from scholarly articles, institutional reports, and case studies across various African nations, including Kenya, Rwanda, and Tanzania. Findings reveal that decentralized solar solutions, such as mini-grids and standalone solar home systems, offer scalable and costeffective alternatives to grid expansion. However, challenges such. Ydf as high upfront costs, weak regulatory frameworks, and limited financing mechanisms hinder widespread adoption. Innovative financing models, including pay-as-you-go (PAYG) schemes and microcredit financing, have demonstrated success in increasing energy affordability, while public-private partnerships (PPPs) have facilitated large-scale solar electrification projects. The study concludes that achieving universal energy access in rural Africa requires strengthened institutional support, policy harmonization, and increased investment in decentralized renewable energy solutions. Policy recommendations include government-led subsidy programs, tax incentives for solar enterprises, and enhanced regulatory frameworks to encourage private sector participation. This…

items.title: A hybrid predictive and uncertainty-aware framework for renewable hydrogen system efficiency assessment and sustainable energy planning
items.summary_raw: Abstract Renewable hydrogen is emerging as a critical element in the transition toward low-carbon and sustainable energy systems; however, accurately evaluating system efficiency remains challenging due to complex, nonlinear interactions among technical and environmental factors. This study proposes a hybrid predictive and uncertainty-aware framework for assessing renewable hydrogen system efficiency and supporting sustainable energy planning. The framework integrates Elastic Net and Extra Trees regression models enhanced through meta-heuristic optimization using Sparrow Search and Firefly algorithms to improve predictive performance. Recursive Feature Elimination is applied to identify the most influential variables governing system behavior, while Dempster–Shafer Theory is incorporated to model uncertainty and construct a robust ensemble prediction strategy. The proposed approach is evaluated using a dataset of 2,535 renewable hydrogen system records with spatial attributes derived from documented geographical coordinates. Experimental results demonstrate notable improvements in predictive accuracy, with a 12% increase in R² and a 15% reduction in MAE compared to baseline approaches. Sensitivity analysis indicates that photovoltaic power generation and electrolysis efficiency are the most influential factors affecting hydrogen system performance. Beyond improved prediction accuracy, the framework provides interpretable insights that can support infrastructure development…

items.title: Model for Land Use Control in Agricultural Areas to Support Food Self-Sufficiency by 2045 in Demak Regency
