items.title: The effect of Energy Consumption, Renewable Energy, and Circular Energy on economic growth in Nigeria
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: This study investigates the effect of energy consumption, renewable energy, and circular energy on Nigeria’s economic growth using an ex-post facto research design. Time series data from 2010 to 2023 were sourced from Statista and the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Statistical Bulletin. The study employed various statistical tools, including Descriptive Statistics, Group Unit Root Test, Johansen Cointegration Test, and the Vector Error Correction Model (VECM), with post-analysis tests ensuring model validity. Findings revealed that primary energy consumption had an insignificant positive effect on economic growth due to inefficiencies, transmission losses, and over-reliance on fossil fuels. Total renewable energy capacity also showed a positive but insignificant impact, indicating its potential in driving economic expansion with adequate investment and policy support. However, circular energy exhibited a negative effect, highlighting Nigeria’s underdeveloped recycling capacity and the need for technological advancements. The study concludes that energy plays a vital role in economic growth but requires a diversified and efficient strategy to maximize its benefits. It recommends upgrading energy infrastructure to enhance efficiency, increasing investments in renewable energy through incentives and financing options, and fostering circular energy innovations via policy frameworks, financial incentives, and research development. By addressing these areas, Nigeria can achieve a…

items.title: Artificial intelligence-Driven Renewable Energy Solutions for Rural Electrification in Africa
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: This research examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in advancing renewable energy solutions for rural electrification in Africa, where energy access remains a critical challenge. The study adopts a qualitative research approach, utilizing secondary data from academic journals, industry reports, and case studies. Comparative analysis is applied to assess AI-driven electrification projects and their effectiveness in rural settings. The paper explores AI technologies such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and smart grid optimization in renewable energy applications like energy demand forecasting, smart grid management, and predictive maintenance. Case studies from Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa highlight successful implementations of AI in solar mini-grids, wind energy projects, and battery storage solutions. In Nigeria, AI-powered mini-grids optimize energy generation and storage, ensuring consistent power supply in off-grid areas. In Kenya, AI supports wind forecasting and grid management, increasing the efficiency of the Lake Turkana Wind Power Project. In South Africa, AI-driven battery storage systems enhance the reliability of energy distribution by predicting optimal charging and discharging cycles. Despite these advancements, the study identifies challenges such as high initial costs, technical expertise gaps, and regulatory barriers, which hinder scalability. The paper offers recommendations for addressing these challenges, including investment…

items.title: Enforcement drives conservation policy impacts at the Brazilian agricultural frontier
items.summary_raw: Why do forest conservation policies work in some contexts but not in others? Here we empirically evaluate how the effectiveness of complementary conservation policy instruments layered onto command-and-control forest regulation depends on environmental law enforcement. We exploit a biome-based policy assignment rule that created policy discontinuities along the official Amazon-Cerrado boundary in Brazil. We find that Amazon-specific governance innovations are associated with reductions in forest loss, while effects on land-use intensification, measured as pasture-to-cropland conversion, are weaker and less systematic. Crucially, these effects vary depending on how intensively environmental authorities enforce the underlying forest law on the ground. Our findings highlight that complementary conservation policy instruments work best when environmental authorities let punishment follow closely on the heels of the crime.

items.title: Combining storylines of energy citizenship with narratives of future-world evolutions to design transformative and socially informed energy transition scenarios
items.summary_raw: Despite a growing body of research seeking to integrate social sciences into scenario-based research and modelling, climate policy analysis remains largely dominated by top-down approaches that underrepresent the sociopolitical dimensions of the energy transition, particularly at the local level. In this context, the concept of energy citizenship has gained increasing attention as a means of fostering more inclusive, democratic, and equitable energy systems. However, significant gaps exist regarding its conceptual clarity, operationalisation, and systematic integration into scenario-based research and modelling practices. This study addresses these gaps by presenting a novel interdisciplinary framework for transformative scenario design that explicitly links social innovations of energy citizenship with alternative future-world evolutions. We deconstruct energy citizenship into distinct patterns and trends and translate them into people-centred storylines that capture diverse forms of individual and collective engagement in the energy transition. These storylines are embedded within three future-world narratives inspired by the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, while describing alternative long-term pathways in which citizen agency, social practices, and collective action play the central role. We construct a multilayered scenario space that enables systematic exploration of decarbonisation pathways informed by empirical research clarifying the concept of energy citizenship…

items.title: Citizen priorities among energy transition objectives and support for energy generation technologies
items.summary_raw: The transformation of energy systems requires decisions and public support across multiple levels, from broad energy transition goals to the implementation of local projects. Existing studies link support to environmental beliefs or political ideology, yet often treat technologies in coarse categories or rely on single-issue measures. This study addresses this gap by examining how individuals’ priorities among energy transition objectives and ideological orientations jointly structure acceptance of different energy generation technologies. Using data from a 2024 survey experiment conducted in Switzerland, respondents completed structured pairwise comparisons between key objectives of the energy transition: biodiversity, emissions, land use, electricity imports and savings, and price. These comparisons were used to derive individual priorities. Together with measures of political ideology, these priorities are linked to technology-specific acceptance ratings in a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for repeated evaluations within individuals. The results show that technology acceptance is shaped by multiple, partially independent belief-based trade-off dimensions rather than a single renewable-fossil divide. Even technologies commonly grouped together, such as renewable energy sources, are associated with distinct constellations of priorities. Moreover, political ideology explains additional variation beyond belief-based trade-offs, indicating technology-specific…

items.title: Promoters, practitioners, hopers, independents and adversaries: reflections on the dominant expert narrative in Czech climate communication
From concept to practice: Patient safety culture and patient safety climate in dentistry
items.summary_raw: Research on safety culture and safety climate in dentistry is limited, leading to gaps in understanding and implementation. Therefore, this literature review examined the significance of patient safety culture and safety climate in dentistry, emphasizing their contributions to enhancing the quality of dental care and mitigating adverse events. Patient safety lapses in dentistry include mistakes in procedures, diagnoses, communication, and equipment, and they are often caused by people, systems, and the environment. Safety culture refers to the rules and guidelines that govern how a healthcare organization is structured, while safety climate refers to the attitudes and behaviors common in everyday practice. These ideas are connected, so they need to be addressed together. Essential strategies to enhance safety culture and climate include (1) leadership; (2) education and training for personnel and patients; (3) effective communication and non-punitive reporting mechanisms; (4) standardization through protocols and checklists; (5) teamwork and collaboration; (6) patient engagement; (7) technological advancements such as electronic health records and incident reporting systems; and (8) continuous improvement through audits and performance metrics. To make dentistry safer for patients, we need to move from separate treatments to more unified ones. The field of dentistry can move beyond reactive measures and create a culture where safety is a top priority for everyone by making…

items.title: From belief to intention: perceived tourist effectiveness and low-carbon tourism in tourism cities
items.summary_raw: This study examines how tourists form low-carbon tourism (LCT) intentions in tourism cities by identifying the belief-level mechanisms underlying motivational formation. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behaviour with a Cognition–Affect–Conation perspective, perceived tourist effectiveness (PTE) is positioned as a cognitive antecedent of attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control. Survey data from tourists in major Vietnamese tourism cities were analysed using PLS-SEM. Results show that PTE is positively related to all three TPB components and has significant indirect effects on LCT intention through each, with attitude and perceived behavioural control representing the strongest pathways. Multigroup analysis further indicates generational differences in the belief–motivation process. The study contributes to urban tourism research by examining the visitor-level side of low-carbon transitions in tourism cities.

items.title: Aligned and discordant profiles of nursing informatics competency and information-security attitudes among clinical nurses: a single-centre study in China
items.summary_raw: Background Secure digital nursing practice requires both nursing informatics competency and favourable information-security attitudes, yet these domains may not develop in parallel within individual nurses. This study aimed to identify joint profiles of nursing informatics competency and information-security attitudes among clinical nurses, examine characteristics associated with profile membership, and compare nurse-perceived nurse–patient relationship quality across profiles. Methods A single-centre cross-sectional survey was conducted among a convenience sample of 1,149 clinical nurses at a tertiary hospital in China between February and June 2026. Latent profile analysis used nine standardised competency and attitude dimensions. Three-step analyses examined profile correlates and differences in nurse-perceived nurse–patient relationship quality. A complementary configurational analysis examined combinations associated with high and non-high relationship quality. Results Six competency–attitude profiles were identified, comprising aligned low and high patterns, two contrasting discordant patterns and two mixed patterns. A more favourable perceived hospital ethical climate was consistently associated with the high competency–high attitude profile, which retained the highest adjusted nurse-perceived nurse–patient relationship quality, although between-profile differences were attenuated after adjustment. High competency–high attitude profile membership combined with a…

items.title: Mind the mismatch: mapping stakeholder-interest divergence in urban e-mobility across major western anglophone arenas using large language models
items.source_name: Transportation Research Part A Policy and Practice
items.summary_raw: Urban e-mobility has emerged as a cornerstone of sustainability transitions, yet electric vehicle (EV) adoption has slowed in key markets despite robust policy support, exposing societal tensions in transition governance, and more fundamentally, a persistent gap in understanding how stakeholder-interest misalignments may erode the legitimacy of climate action itself. This research examines stakeholder-interest divergence as an indicator of potential coordination friction in e-mobility transitions, focusing on how government, academia, news media and the public within major Anglophone discursive arenas articulate differing priorities, framings, and concerns. Drawing on a corpus of Western-centric policy documents, scholarly articles, news stories and social-media posts from 2020 to 2024, we deploy a large language model (LLM) pipeline to analyse topic salience and sentiment across discursive arenas. Results show that government and academic arenas devote less than 3% of their coverage to user experience and maintenance, concerns that dominate public discussion, while concentrating on incentives, regulation and technological advance. News media appear to follow the same institutional pattern, reported as an exploratory signal given the lower cross-model consistency of that corpus. In negative narratives, news outlets attribute opposition to subsidy shortfalls, likewise an exploratory signal, while citizens emphasize persistent cost gaps under current tax regimes, helping…

items.title: Behaviour-Based Decision Making and Willingness to Pay for Low-Carbon Fuels in India’s Transport Sector
items.source_name: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
items.summary_raw: An estimated 22% of global greenhouse gas emissions result from the transportation industry, due principally to long-haul freight's reliance on fossil fuel. India's economy is growing faster than ever before, with an increasing demand for logistics; hence, the emission from the road transport sector is also on the rise. Thus, decarbonization has now an indispensable component of the nation’s action against climate change. This study examines the decision-making process of individuals and/or corporates in India’s long-haul truck segment and their willingness to pay for low-carbon fuels. By employing a mixed-methods approach, the study investigates the influence of climate awareness, behavioral attitudes, cost sensitivity, risk perception, and social norms on fuel choice. Through a structured questionnaire, primary data was collected from fleet owners, transport managers long haul truck drivers and a small sample of consumers. Secondary data was collected from policy report and academic studies. The awareness of climate change may be much higher than the actual responses. Many people know a lot about climate issues, but they are unwilling to pay for low-carbon fuels because they are more sensitive to price and more mindful of risks in infrastructure and operations. Nonetheless, social norms and client pressure can lead some people towards cleaner fuels. The study calls for a combination of policy coherence and market-driven approaches alongside behavioral efforts to enhance…

items.title: Promoting sustainable travel intentions: the effect of information nudges
items.summary_raw: Introduction Tourism contributes substantially to global greenhouse gas emissions. To reduce travel-related carbon emissions, a shift toward more sustainable travel choices is urgently needed. Research has consistently shown a significant gap between environmental attitudes and sustainable travel behaviors. Yet, it has proven difficult to promote sustainable travel behavior without understanding and narrowing the gap between environmental attitudes and sustainable travel intentions. This study examines the effect of information nudges to support the shift toward more climate-friendly travel intentions. Methods We conducted randomized choice experiments among a large sample of German holidaymakers ( n = 2,186), covering the three main segments of German vacation demand: domestic/proximity tourism, mid-range Mediterranean travel, and long-haul travel. Participants first self-selected their preferred travel segment, allowing for realistic decision-making scenarios, and were then randomly assigned to one of three carbon-related information nudges or a baseline condition without additional information. We examined the effects of the nudges on transport and accommodation choices. Results The results indicate that carbon-related information can influence specific travel choices toward more climate-friendly alternatives, although effects were not consistently observed across all contexts and nudges. Significant effects were found particularly for transport choices in Mediterranean…

items.title: Climate Change is Rewriting the Hydroclimatic Operating Envelope of Mines
items.summary_raw: Physical climate risk in mining is framed as floods, droughts, heatwaves, and wildfires acting on assets with fixed design conditions. We argue that the deeper change is a moving hydroclimatic operating envelope: climate alters the water and heat conditions around mines, while geology, engineering, and lifecycle stage govern how those changes propagate. Linking a global mine inventory to observed and projected Köppen-Geiger classes shows that 16.2% of 1093 geocoded mines changed climate subtype between 1901-1930 and 1991-2020. By 2071-2099, the share rises to 29.8% under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2-4.5 (SSP2-4.5) and 42.5% under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 (SSP5-8.5). Water trajectories also separate. Under SSP5-8.5, median precipitation falls by 3.1% at arid mines but rises by 6.5% at humid locations, while precipitation seasonality increases in arid regions. Commodity geography stratifies this exposure, whereas mine method alone provides little adjusted separation. Tailings records place weather within multi-causal failure pathways: 64 of 229 failures with a reported cause included a weather hazard, yet raise categories did not distinguish reported climate-assessment responses. Literature links these shifts to pore pressure, infiltration, heat, material evolution, water storage, and post-closure hydrology. The combined evidence supports adaptation based on monitored, scenario-conditioned operating envelopes rather than static hazard checklists.

items.title: Climate change education in primary schools: knowledge, attitudes and pro-environmental behaviour of students in Greece
items.source_name: International Research in Geographical and Environmental Education
items.summary_raw: Climate change education plays a crucial role in shaping children’s environmental understanding and engagement, particularly at the primary school level. This study examines Greek primary school students’ climate change knowledge, attitudes, and pro-environmental behavior within the Knowledge–Attitude–Behavior (KAB) framework. A quantitative survey was conducted with 711 students from nine public primary schools in Greece using an age-appropriate questionnaire. Results revealed strong environmental and climate change attitudes and relatively high pro-environmental behavior, while climate change knowledge was moderate and uneven, with persistent misconceptions related to mitigation. Boys scored higher in knowledge, whereas girls showed stronger environmental attitudes and behaviors. Younger students (Grade 5; aged 11 years) demonstrated higher knowledge levels, while older students (Grade 6; aged 12 years) exhibited more positive environmental attitudes. Moreover, environmental and climate change attitudes were the strongest predictors of pro-environmental behavior, with knowledge exerting a smaller indirect effect. The study underscores the need for educational approaches that integrate conceptual learning with affective engagement and action-oriented experiences. Consequently, it provides evidence relevant to curriculum design and environmental education policy in a Mediterranean context, where climate-related risks are intensifying and remain underrepresented in primary…

items.title: Exploring the Interplay of Freshwater Resources, Renewable Energy, and Decarbonization on Education in G20 Nations
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT This study aims to empirically examine the role of carbon emissions (CEM), freshwater resources (FWR), agriculture, forestry, and fisheries resources (AFFR), renewable energy consumption (RENE), financial inclusion (FINC), and technological innovation (TCI) on education (EDC) of the G20 member states during the period of 2000–2023. As the main estimation method, this study uses the MMQR. In addition, the robustness of the results is measured using the CS‐ARDL model along with a control function approach. According to the MMQR results, CEM, FWR, RENE, and FINC positively affect EDC across most quantiles, while AFFR exerts a negative effect throughout the distribution. TCI negatively influences lower and middle quantiles but becomes positive at higher quantiles. The CS‐ARDL findings confirm the positive long‐run effects of FWR, RENE, and FINC, the negative effects of CEM and AFFR, and a negative short‐run but positive long‐run effect of TCI. The control function results further indicate the relevance of accounting for potential endogeneity associated with FINC and AFFR. This study makes several contributions to the existing literature by considering education as a dependent variable in a sustainability‐technology approach.

items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: The growing transition to renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal, presents significant challenges due to their intermittent nature, requiring advanced optimization strategies for efficient integration into existing power systems. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in addressing these challenges by enhancing energy forecasting, optimizing smart grid operations, and improving predictive maintenance. This study employs a secondary research methodology, conducting a qualitative analysis of existing literature, case studies, and technical reports on AI applications in renewable energy optimization. The study explores how machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and reinforcement learning (RL) enhance energy forecasting, real-time grid management, and fault detection. AI-driven models improve the accuracy of solar and wind energy predictions, allowing better supply-demand balancing. Additionally, AI-powered smart grids enhance energy distribution, reduce wastage, and increase grid reliability. AI also enables predictive maintenance, minimizing operational costs and infrastructure failures. The research is grounded in Systems Theory, Optimization Theory, and Technological Determinism, offering a structured framework for analyzing AI’ s impact on renewable energy systems. items.title: Is Trump Trying to Blow Up the Permitting Deal?
items.summary_raw: This is Heatmap Daily, an evening news digest written by our executive editor. Subscribe here. Updated, 11:05 p.m. ET At the end of the day, the biggest threat to the bipartisan permitting deal probably isn’t green groups, the fossil fuel industry, or monopoly utilities. It’s President Trump himself. The legislative proposal is meant to constrain the president from tampering with clean energy projects — and if it passes, then some of its provisions seem like they could do so. More broadly, the administration has to make a show of good faith that it will return to what Whitehouse has called “regular order” on wind and solar permits. items.title: How to Sue an Energy Project After the Permitting Bill
items.summary_raw: A bipartisan group of senators proposed major reforms to the country’s environmental laws last month in an effort to speed up the federal approval process for energy projects of all kinds. If it passes, one of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act’s biggest changes would be transforming the U.S. court system’s role in federal environmental reviews. The bill would constrain who can challenge federal environmental decisions in court, which courts can hear those challenges, what plaintiffs can argue in those cases, and what remedies are available when the plaintiffs win. In particular, it would become a lot more difficult — though not impossible — for outside groups to stop construction on a project or vacate a permit if they deemed it to be environmentally risky. Part of the motivation for the bill, at least among Democrats, is the idea that the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, has become a significant obstacle to building clean energy projects and the infrastructure required to connect them to the grid. The bill includes a number of changes to NEPA that would expedite environmental reviews and prevent legal challenges under NEPA from dragging out project timelines. items.title: Why Google is paying to upgrade nuclear power plants
items.summary_raw: Last week, the Georgia Public Service Commission voted to approve a new deal between Georgia Power and the tech giant Google. Starting in 2028, Google will help pay for upgrades to the state’s nuclear reactors. “So, around 100 megawatts of carbon-free energy, paid for by somebody else,” PSC Commissioner Stan Wise said to staffers shortly before the vote. “Why don’t you bring us some more of those deals?” Georgia Power wants to upgrade four of the state’s older nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch so they can produce more energy. State regulators approved the Vogtle upgrades last year, but the specifics of how to pay for the work weren’t hashed out. Now, the commission has voted to move ahead with the updates at Plant Hatch too — and approved a new subscription program so large customers like Google can pay for both. “We appreciate Google’s continued leadership in this space and partnership in developing this program, which we see as the latest example of how large-load growth can benefit all electric customers,” said Aaron Mitchell, senior vice president of strategic growth for Georgia Power, in a statement. Under the program, Google will pay a subscription fee on top of its electricity bill to help cover the cost of the nuclear upgrades. In exchange, Google gets credit toward its goal of using only carbon-free energy by 2030. items.title: A federal program to restore forests after disaster has gotten too many funding requests
items.summary_raw: Federal money meant to help restore forests after disasters has stopped flowing because of a lack of funding. According to the Michigan office of the federal Farm Service Agency, the Emergency Forest Restoration Program, or EFRP, has received more requests for aid around the country than it can pay out. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Agriculture — where the farm agency is housed — confirmed the news. “Currently, requests for financial assistance through the Emergency Forest Restoration Program exceed the funding currently available,” the USDA spokesperson said. Created by Congress in 2008 as part of the national Farm Bill, EFRP provides disaster relief to landowners restoring nonindustrial forests. Almost two years ago, Congress appropriated $357 million for the program “ to remain available until expended .” The USDA earmarked much of that money for landowners dealing with lingering damage from the monster 2024 Atlantic hurricane season . In Michigan, property owners whose forests were compromised by a 2025 ice storm were invited to apply . But the rollout of the federal program in the Mitten State has been mired in delays, confusion about eligibility , and what’s been described by landowners and foresters as little communication from federal officials. items.title: How import tariffs on China's new energy vehicles affect host countries’ energy transition
items.summary_raw: The global energy transition increasingly relies on new energy vehicles (NEVs) to facilitate renewable energy integration. China's exports of NEVs play a pivotal role in addressing the rising global energy transition demand. As economies are imposing tariffs on imported China's NEVs to protect their own domestic industries, a critical question remains underexplored: do these tariff policies shape host countries’ energy transition? This study employs a panel threshold model to investigate the threshold effect of import tariffs targeting China's NEVs on the share of renewable energy in primary energy use. Using panel data from 103 economies over 2017–2023, we confirm the existence of a critical threshold. Below this level, tariffs positively influence energy transition by complementing domestic NEV research and development (R&D), reducing R&D costs and enabling greater investment in transition initiatives. Beyond the threshold, tariffs hinder energy transition by limiting NEV imports and redirecting resources toward costly domestic NEV R&D, which crowds out energy transition fundings. The findings highlight the importance of optimal tariff design, particularly for low-income economies, to balance protection of domestic NEV industries with the need to leverage technology spillovers and accelerate energy transition.

The technological determinism theory was anchored in this study. This study adopted a qualitative research method, utilising in-depth interviews to explore the role of artificial intelligence in public affairs communication for climate policy advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The population of the study consisted of 120 key stakeholders involved in climate policy advocacy and governance, including government officials, policymakers, environmental NGOs, media professionals and AI experts. The sample size comprised 20 purposively selected respondents with expertise in climate policy, artificial intelligence applications in governance and public affairs communication. The sampling technique used was purposive sampling, allowing the selection of individuals who possess specialized knowledge and experience relevant to the study. The method of data collection involves semi-structured, in-depth interviews and method of data analysis followed thematic analysis, where transcribed interview data were systematically coded to identify emerging patterns, themes and relationships. The findings revealed that, AI-driven tools significantly enhance public affairs communication by improving message dissemination, audience targeting and engagement strategies in climate advocacy. items.title: A Predictive Model of Bullying Perpetration Towards Students with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities in Physical Education: The Role of Motivation, Tolerance and Attitudes
items.summary_raw: Bullying towards students with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) remains a persistent problem in school contexts, yet the psychosocial mechanisms underlying bullying perpetration in inclusive settings are still insufficiently understood. Primarily grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) as a complementary framework for considering attitudinal variables, this study examined a predictive model of bullying perpetration towards students with SEND in Physical Education (PE), focusing on the role of motivational and attitudinal processes. A total of 356 secondary school students (M age = 13.77; SD = 1.34) completed measures assessing perceived teaching style, basic psychological needs satisfaction, self-determined motivation, tolerance, attitudes towards disability, and bullying perpetration towards peers with disabilities. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlational analyses, and path analysis. Results showed that higher levels of self-determined motivation were positively associated with tolerance and more positive attitudes towards disability. In turn, tolerance and attitudes towards disability negatively predicted bullying perpetration. In this case, self-determined motivation did not directly predict bullying perpetration but showed an indirect association through its effects on tolerance and attitudes. These findings highlight the importance of motivational and attitudinal pathways in…

items.title: A Transformation in Utilizing CO₂ as an Energy Source and its Economic Importance
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Article co-authored while at the Federal University of Technology, Akure, on carbon dioxide (CO₂) capture and utilization (CCU) as an alternative to treating CO₂ only as waste, with attention to opportunities, applications, and economic importance in the Nigerian and global energy context. Originally presented at the 39th Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists (NAPE) Annual International Conference and Exhibition, Lagos, Nigeria, 18–21 November 2021 (Books of Abstract and Conference Proceeding, p. 56), and published in the NAPE Bulletin (Journal of the Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists). items.title: Public perceptions and (lack of) support for mitigation of artificial light at night in coastal cities
items.summary_raw: Artificial light at night (ALAN) is an expanding environmental pressure in urban areas, yet effective mitigation depends on public support. We investigated how residents of two Chilean coastal cities perceive ALAN, its impacts and potential mitigation measures. Respondents demonstrated asymmetric environmental literacy, recognising the societal benefits of lighting while showing limited awareness of its ecological consequences, particularly for coastal-marine ecosystems. Support for mitigation depended on preserving valued social benefits, with greater environmental literacy associated with stronger acceptance of mitigation measures. Findings suggest that perceptions of safety, aesthetic value and institutional responsibility shape policy acceptance, highlighting the need to balance nature conservation with societal objectives. Rather than viewing ALAN as a technical lighting issue, we frame it as a social-ecological governance challenge. We argue that successful ALAN mitigation will require integrating environmental education, participatory decision-making and collaborative governance to achieve lighting policies that are both publicly acceptable and ecologically effective.

items.title: Transcending sports: public demand for gender equity in name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy and its connection to the diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policy debate in higher education
items.summary_raw: Abstract Public demand suggests that salience and opinion shape how individuals interpret policy, creating openings for framing and value branding to influence those views. I apply this framework to assess public demand for gender equity in name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy and examine how it aligns with the broader debate in higher education concerning diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Using survey data from 1,510 respondents across five states, I find that attitudes toward DEI significantly structure views of gender equity in NIL. Public demand for equity in NIL follows traditional predictors, including political ideology, age, education, and gender, while support for college sports has an unexpected negative association. I also identify foundational connections between NIL and support for regulating diversity and equity in higher education, suggesting that NIL functions as an emerging equity policy domain shaped by the same political and cultural forces that structure views of DEI.

items.title: IONOSPHERIC TECHNOLOGY, CLIMATE CHANGE, ENERGY MARKETS AND INTERNATIONAL COORDINATION A load-bearing interdisciplinary framework for climate attribution, disclosure narratives, and the geopolitics of hidden energy claims
Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Shaping Climate Adaptation among Smallholder Leafy Vegetable Agripreneurs in Semi-Arid Tanzania
items.summary_raw: Climate change adaptation research among smallholder farmers has primarily focused on staple crops, leaving leafy vegetables underrepresented despite their contributions to nutrition, income, local markets, and resilience in semi-arid farming systems. This study examined climate change knowledge, attitudes, and adaptation practices among smallholder leafy vegetable agripreneurs in Dodoma City and Singida Municipality, central Tanzania. It also examined associations between individual adaptation practices, socio-demographic characteristics, and leafy vegetable types. A cross-sectional survey of 385 agripreneurs was conducted across four wards using face-to-face interviews guided by an expanded Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice framework. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Friedman tests, cross-tabulations, chi-square tests, and Cramér's V effect sizes. Agripreneurs demonstrated substantial knowledge of drought, rainfall variability, rising temperatures, and pest and disease outbreaks and expressed favourable attitudes towards adaptation. Comparatively accessible practices, including compost or manure application, intercropping, mixed or relay cropping, crop rotation, crop diversification, and drought-tolerant or early-maturing varieties, were more widely established than greenhouse farming, drip irrigation, and integrated pest management. Individual adaptation practices were significantly associated with selected socio-demographic characteristics and leafy…

items.title: How Does Carbon Offsetting Affect Firms' Emitting Behaviour? Global Evidence
items.source_name: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT In light of the growing emphasis on corporate carbon reduction efforts, this study investigates the effectiveness of carbon offsetting in curbing corporate pollution levels using a global sample of firms. The analysis indicates that carbon offsetting is positively associated with corporate carbon emissions. I document that carbon offsetting could hinder corporate efforts to reduce carbon emissions. Furthermore, the continental location of firms is also an important consideration when evaluating the dynamics of this relationship. For firms in Asia, the positive impact of carbon offsets on carbon emissions is even greater. However, being in North America mitigates the relationship between carbon offsets and firm greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, in evaluating whether country‐level institutional quality can be harnessed to enhance the potential deliverables of carbon offsetting schemes, I find limited evidence that countries can leverage regulatory quality to improve their outcomes. Perception of corruption, the rule of law and government effectiveness do not appear to matter. The results are robust to alternative econometric specifications.

When the storm hits: how does energy uncertainty influence green credit in Chinese banks?
items.summary_raw: General economic policy uncertainty is known to suppress credit, yet the specific impact of energy-related uncertainty on sustainable finance remains underexplored. This study investigates the influence of the Energy Uncertainty Index (EUI) on Green Credit (GC) allocation within the Chinese banking sector. Using an unbalanced panel of 42 A-share-listed commercial banks from 2011 to 2023, we employ an import-share-weighted Geopolitical Risk (GPR) index as an instrumental variable and System GMM estimation to address endogeneity. Our results demonstrate that (i) heightened EUI prompts banks to structurally shift credit from carbon-intensive to green industries; (ii) panel quantile regression reveals that institutions with a stronger initial green credit base respond more vigorously to energy shocks; and (iii)the mechanism is robustly driven by a supply-side transmission channel—Peer Green Credit Pressure (PGCP)—while also providing empirical evidence consistent with a demand-side pull from corporate Green Investment Intensity (GI). Heterogeneity tests indicate this reallocation is most pronounced among state-owned banks, large-scale institutions, and banks in green finance pilot zones. These findings challenge the conventional view that uncertainty uniformly inhibits lending, illustrating instead that targeted energy uncertainty acts as a catalyst for green credit restructuring and enhances energy transition resilience.

items.title: Reviewing the implementation design of energy subsidy reforms: insights from novel cross-country data
items.summary_raw: Over the past two decades, energy subsidy reforms have increasingly gained importance as mitigation measures to fight climate change. Still, many countries subsidize fossil energy consumption, and reforms are often short-lived. This paper presents harmonized cross-country data on the design of energy subsidy reforms, obtained from a structured literature review of both implemented and failed consumption subsidy reforms between 1978 and 2021. This standardized data enables the identification and validation of key design characteristics, including the motivation for reform, the use of gradual approaches, communication strategies, pricing mechanisms, and social protection measures, as well as their use in implementing reforms. The data highlight significant regional heterogeneity and emphasize the importance of context-specificity in shaping reform designs. The study also demonstrates the connection between key aspects of reform design and reform implementation, as well as associations with subsidy levels. It offers lessons for middle-income countries, especially those planning to implement carbon pricing policies. Lastly, this paper lays the groundwork for future research to explore these factors in greater detail; one avenue is to link design characteristics and political economy factors.KEY POLICY INSIGHTS Many reforms fail to reduce subsidies sustainably, a pattern strongly linked to the pricing mechanisms that countries use. Automatic pricing systems and even liberalised…

items.title: Satellite-based green and blue agricultural water accounting and footprint projections under different climate change scenarios
items.summary_raw: Satellite-based green and blue agricultural water accounting and footprint projections under different climate change scenarios , Garrido-Rubio, Jesús, Gabaldón-Leal, Clara, Galve, Joan M., Antoniadou, Marina, Tassopoulos, Dimitris, Papadaskalopoulou, Christina, González-Piqueras, José

items.title: Substitute oaks: Modeling human-assisted dispersal of climate-threatened foundation species
items.summary_raw: Climate change is causing the global decline of important foundation species, threatening the loss of ecological function. Human-assisted dispersal can mitigate this loss by relocating species to climatically suitable areas beyond their historical ranges. Moving beyond a method of range expansion for climate-threatened species, we adapted this into a substitution-based approach: replacing lost populations with nearby, functionally similar congeners. We tested this framework by modeling the future distributions of seven culturally and functionally important endemic oak ( Quercus ) species across the California Floristic Province and identifying which areas were projected to lose species but could be substituted with another. We found that around 60% of current oak habitat may lose species by the end of the century, with over 30% losing all oaks. Substitution-based assisted dispersal could mitigate this decline, potentially replacing around 10% of current habitat. However, species projected to decline most under climate change were the least viable donors, while oak species projected to remain relatively stable were common donor candidates. We frame substitution-based assisted dispersal as a proactive approach that directs ecosystems toward functionally analogous states while minimizing ecological novelty.

items.title: How justice-framed policy narratives shape citizen engagement: Evidence from a survey experiment on time and capital contributions
items.summary_raw: Under the dual challenges of global climate change and energy crises, the success of energy transition critically depends on substantive citizen engagement to secure social legitimacy and mobilize distributed resources. However, encouraging such engagement requires moving beyond mere material incentives to resonate with citizens' normative values. This study investigates how energy justice framed policy narratives serve as a key communicative mechanism to foster citizens' willingness to contribute time and capital. Based on a survey experiment with 927 participants, the study designed three narratives reflecting distributional, procedural, and recognition justice compared against a control group. The experimental results indicate that justice-framed narratives can significantly enhance citizens’ policy support, thereby promoting willingness to contribute time and capital, with the rights protection narrative representing procedural justice being the most prominent. Moreover, the effects of different justice-framed policy narratives also vary among citizens with different levels of trust in the government. This study advances the theoretical discourse on just energy transition by elucidating the roles of policy narratives, while offering practical insights to guide governmental communication strategies that foster citizen engagement and promote a just and sustainable energy transition.

items.title: A democratic deficit in climate education? Youth experiences and public expectations in Australia
items.summary_raw: Education systems must equip students to navigate futures in a climate-changed world. Yet, climate education remains fragmented and overly focused on scientific knowledge transfer. This can leave young people anxious and excluded from meaningful learning. This paper explores the (mis)alignment between young people’s lived experiences of climate learning and the expectations of the wider public in Australia. We combine survey data from 1,058 adults with qualitative data from 74 young people (aged 11–16). Findings suggest that while both groups value climate education, adults prioritize STEM disciplines, while young people express deep frustration with the system’s narrow scope and demand greater opportunities for civic action, critical discussion, and emotional literacy. The paper argues that reconciling the expectations of society with the lived experiences of young people is essential to renewing the democratic legitimacy and future relevance of education in an era of accelerating environmental and social change.

items.title: The significance of global identity in shaping individual behaviour and policy support: Focus on plastic purchasing and consumption
items.summary_raw: Abstract Background Global identity (GI), a sense of belonging to a global society, is gaining attention as a key factor for promoting pro‐environmental behaviours (PEB) to tackle the global environmental crisis. Among such global predicaments, plastic waste and pollution remain pressing issues. Although prior research has established a link between GI and PEB, the underlying psychological pathways have not been comprehensively explored. Aims Applying the comprehensive action determination model (CADM), the present study aims to develop and test a model that investigates the contribution of GI to PEB via psychological mediators. Additionally, a preliminary examination of the relationship between GI and policy support is conducted. Materials and Methods A web‐based survey was conducted in February 2025 using quota sampling by gender, age and prefecture among Japanese adults ( N = 2400). The questionnaire measured GI, plastic‐related PEB, psychological factors (e.g. awareness of consequence, ascription of responsibility, lack of personal response efficacy and goal intention) and policy support. Results The revised model from structural equation modelling showed acceptable fit, which was in line with the original theoretical expectations. GI showed positive associations with awareness of consequence and ascription of responsibility, and a negative association with lack of personal response efficacy. It also directly influenced goal intention and plastic PEB. A multiple…

items.title: Waste to Energy Landscape: Current milestone for Sustainable Future- Review
items.summary_raw: The volume of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) is predicted to increase to 3.86 billion tons annually by 2050, posing a major danger to urban infrastructure and environmental sustainability. This research summarizes information on the global Waste-to-Energy (WtE) landscape in order to assess the technological, economic, and environmental performance of thermal, thermochemical, and biochemical treatment technologies. Although thermal mass-burn is still the industry standard because of operational issues, this analysis shows a critical trade-off between economic viability and environmental performance, as demonstrated by the superior GHG emission profiles of gasification compared to its higher levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). Although thermal mass-burn is still the industry standard due to operational reliability and sustainability, this analysis reveals a critical trade-off between economic viability and environmental performance, as demonstrated by the superior GHG emission profiles of gasification compared to its higher levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). The study also contrasts "rapid growth" models that prioritize immediate capacity development with "mature" markets that prioritize strict emission compliance and high waste diversion rates, as well as technological constraints that exist in industrialized and developing nations. By highlighting methodological shortcomings in previous research, especially the over-reliance on theoretical lab-scale data vs real-world…

items.title: Blue economy, climate risk, and fisherfolks: an inquiry into the state narrative of blue economy and right of fisherfolks
items.source_name: Journal of Ocean and Coastal Economics
items.summary_raw: The blue economy is an extension of finance capital into the coast and is a larger frontier expansion project. This capital is confronted with climate risks as well. The blue economy creates new economic zones, which fall into a risk zone in which output and productivity deplete over time. The blue economy projects conflict with the declining fisheries resources, which puts the fishing community's life at risk. The policies that promote the blue economy often neglect the resource-dependent communities across the coastal areas.

items.source_name: Proceedings of the Indian National Science Academy

items.title: Revisiting the Carbon Lock-In: Outlining an Agenda on How Affective Polarization Constrains Climate Policy Making
items.summary_raw: Carbon lock-in, the self-reinforcing inertia that perpetuates fossil fuel dependence, emerges from interdependent technological, institutional, economic, and behavioral factors. As climate policy has become increasingly polarized across advanced democracies, the role of affective polarization in reinforcing these barriers remains underexplored. This research agenda asks the following question: How and to what extent does affective polarization sustain the carbon lock-in? Drawing on social identity theory and the carbon lock-in literature, I propose a framework in which affective polarization operates as a cross-cutting process strengthening existing lock-in mechanisms through three pathways: (1) elite framing that activates both institutional distrust and out-group animosity toward pro-climate groups; (2) trust erosion linking vertical (elite–mass) and horizontal (mass–mass) polarization to sustained policy resistance; and (3) self-reinforcing feedback loops between polarizing rhetoric and mass resistance that persist across electoral cycles. Partisan identity sorting can transform climate policies into identity markers, turning otherwise reversible constraints into path-dependent barriers that persist even when policies are economically beneficial or technically effective. The agenda applies specifically to high-polarization contexts and calls for empirical investigation of these mechanisms and of depolarization interventions.

items.title: Demonstrating impact and de-risking: Retrofit industry perspectives on Building Performance Evaluation in the United Kingdom
items.summary_raw: Significant investment is being made to retrofit buildings to meet decarbonisation targets and alleviate fuel poverty globally. The application of Building Performance Evaluation (BPE) in retrofitted dwellings in the UK is often limited to simplistic energy models in the form of Energy Performance Certificates. However, recent technological advances have introduced a range of alternative BPE methods that can gather data from buildings and residents to supplement or inform Energy Performance Certificates. In this study, perspectives from 54 retrofit professionals in the UK were gained through workshops and semi-structured interviews. The data were analysed thematically to understand what methods of BPE were being used, as well as the respective barriers and drivers of their adoption. Participants were familiar with the limitations of Energy Performance Certificates and were frequently using complementary BPE methods to fulfil broader purposes across four categories: support decision making; de-risk retrofits; demonstrate impact; and provide learning and improvement. Specific barriers were identified that limited the utilisation of BPE methods including practical aspects as well as incompatibility with funding schemes and current industry norms. These findings inform a conceptual model of the BPE landscape in retrofit. The model highlights the causes and implications of an underperforming market whilst identifying policy voids that, if addressed, could drive greater BPE uptake…

items.title: GREEN ENERGY MARKETING UNDER GOVERNMENT INCENTIVE SCHEMES: STRATEGIC RESPONSES OF ENERGY FIRMS
items.source_name: Journal of Baku Engineering University Economics and Administration
items.summary_raw: Government incentive schemes have become a pivotal driver of renewable energy growth worldwide, prompting varied strategic responses from energy firms.This study examines how companies adapt their marketing and investment strategies under such incentives, drawing on international examples and data from the last decade.The findings indicate that robust incentive policies (e.g.feed-in tariffs, tax credits, renewable portfolio standards) are correlated with significantly faster growth in renewable energy capacity and encourage firms to pivot towards green energy offerings.Energy firms respond by increasing renewable investments, rebranding with sustainability themes, and leveraging incentives in marketing campaigns to attract consumers and investors.However, the effectiveness of incentives in altering firm behavior is not uniform -some policies lead to transformative change, while others have had limited impact or unintended consequences.By analyzing renewable energy trends in key countries alongside firm-level strategy shifts, the paper highlights the critical role of stable, well-designed incentives in enabling a clean energy transition.It also underscores that firms combining incentive-driven investment with authentic sustainability marketing can achieve competitive advantages.The insights contribute to understanding how public policy and corporate strategy intersect in the renewable energy sector, offering recommendations to policymakers and industry leaders for fostering…

items.title: The underestimated emission reduction effect of green credit: a systematic study based on peer effects
items.summary_raw: Against the backdrop of global efforts to address climate change and advance the low-carbon transition, green credit is widely regarded as a financial instrument that directs financial resources toward low-carbon activities. However, most existing studies focus on the direct effects of green credit on individual firms while overlooking interactions among firms. This study systematically examines the peer effects of green credit on corporate carbon reduction at the industry and city levels and explores the underlying mechanisms. To this end, a theoretical model is developed to explain how green credit induces peer effects on corporate carbon reduction. The theoretical predictions are then tested using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms. The results show that greater access to green credit among peer firms significantly reduces the carbon emission intensity of focal firms, indicating that green credit generates carbon-reduction peer effects at both the industry and city levels. Market competition and learning and imitation are important mechanisms through which these peer effects operate. The carbon-reduction peer effects of green credit are more pronounced among firms in industries not subject to green-credit restrictions and among those located in Green Finance Reform and Innovation Pilot Zones. This study advances theoretical modeling and empirical research on green finance and corporate peer effects and provides useful evidence for policymakers seeking to reassess…

items.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Barriers to Climate Change Adaptation Among Secondary School Students in Juba, South Sudan
items.source_name: African Journal of Climate Change and Resource Sustainability
items.summary_raw: Climate change poses significant environmental, social, and economic challenges globally, with particularly severe implications for vulnerable countries such as South Sudan. Secondary school students are an important group in climate-change adaptation because they are directly affected by climate-related hazards and can contribute to adaptive responses in their schools and communities. This mixed-methods study examined the influence of knowledge, attitudes, and barriers on climate-change adaptation among secondary school students in Juba, South Sudan. A purposive sample of 10 public, private, and faith-based secondary schools was selected. From each school, 20 students aged 18 years and above (n = 200) and two key informants, comprising head teachers or senior teachers, participated. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires, while qualitative data were obtained through key-informant interviews. The findings established that knowledge, attitudes, and barriers jointly explained 45.7% of the variation in climate-change adaptation, while 54.3% was explained by other factors outside the model. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F = 53.51, p < 0.001). Knowledge had a positive and significant influence on adaptation (B = 0.178, β = 0.154, p = 0.038), as did attitude (B = 0.151, β = 0.146, p = 0.014). Conversely, barriers had a significant negative influence (B = −0.317, β = −0.293, p < 0.001) and were the strongest predictor of…

items.title: Have billionaires become more tax-friendly since the financial crisis?
items.summary_raw: This article introduces the billionaire tax speech dataset, which provides comprehensive data on the tax speech acts of the hundred richest billionaires living in democracies over the past three decades. It has four major findings. First, the majority of these billionaires did speak publicly about wealth-based taxation, and the extent to which they did so rose explosively after the 2008 financial crisis. Second, while the billionaires became much more likely to weigh in, they have not become more tax-friendly in their public statements. In the first years after the financial crisis pro-tax speech outweighed anti-tax speech, but the trend has since been in the opposite direction. Third, there has, however, been a continuous rise in self-justifying speech: statements that sought to justify a billionaire's own tax record against concrete or diffuse allegations, since the publication of the Panama Papers in 2016. Finally, the terms of debate have shifted. Before the crisis, anti-tax billionaires were still seeking to slash wealth-based taxes further, while pro-tax billionaires sought to retain them. Afterwards, pro-tax billionaires pushed for new or higher wealth-based taxes, and anti-tax billionaires were more often on the defensive, opposing new or more taxation.

items.title: Beyond the equations: Integrating political economy into modelling green-growth pathways for low- and middle-income countries
items.summary_raw: Energy system models are increasingly used to guide infrastructure planning and energy and climate policy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Yet these models are predominantly built around technical and economic assumptions that inadequately account for the political and institutional realities that shape whether modelling outputs are adopted and implemented. This perspective addresses that gap by presenting structured guidelines for integrating political economy analysis throughout the energy system modelling process. The guidelines focus on what needs to be considered at each stage, and signposts to theories and frameworks that can guide implementation. Drawing on the complementary expertise of political economists and modellers, and grounded in experiences across diverse LMIC settings, the guidelines inform seven stages of the modelling process: 1) problem definition, 2) model selection and world view, 3) data collection, 4) assumption setting and scenario development, 5) calibration and interpretation, 6) policy recommendation development, and 7) communication and engagement. The guidelines encourage iterative, reflexive and collaborative practices rather than a mechanical procedure. They emphasise stakeholder co-creation and transparency in model assumptions, along with sensitivity to power dynamics, institutional constraints, and political feasibility. We contend that the purpose of modelling is not solely to identify optimal solutions but to facilitate…

items.title: Enhancing fairness in climate action through policy packages
items.summary_raw: Abstract Achieving a fair transition to climate neutrality requires a careful balancing of policy options. Here we quantitatively evaluate the equity implications of different European Union climate policy packages, considering pricing, regulation via standards, subsidies and transfers. Leveraging an integrated modelling framework, we show that standards limit impact variability within income groups, whereas carbon pricing with transfer-based revenue recycling offsets regressive impacts between income groups. Restricting climate policy implementation to either option, therefore, gives rise to a trade-off between horizontal and vertical equity. We then demonstrate numerically how a multi-instrument budget-neutral policy package can resolve this trade-off. Adopting a broader equity perspective that encompasses both horizontal and vertical equity shifts the preferred policy mix towards a combination of standards, pricing, subsidies and transfers. These results provide an explicit, quantified, equity-based rationale for the adoption and acceptability of comprehensive climate policy packages, offering a more nuanced view on policy design.

items.title: A balanced set of standardized affective environmental images for climate change research
items.summary_raw: Evocative visual imagery is central to research on affective pathways of environmental engagement, yet existing stimulus sets often overrepresent negative imagery and make it difficult to compare positive and negative affective responses under comparable conditions. We developed a balanced database of affective environmental images designed to support controlled comparisons of positive and negative environmental imagery. In total, 587 participants rated 203 images depicting consequences of unmitigated climate change and context-matched positive alternatives on pleasantness and activation. Participants also reported belief in human caused climate change, perceived risk of climate change, and environmental values. The image set covered a broad range of pleasantness while positive and negative images showed comparable activation levels. Across stimuli, pleasantness and activation were quadratically related, consistent with affective stimulus sets spanning over positive and negative valence. Trial-level analyses showed that stronger biospheric values and higher risk perception predicted more negative and more activating responses to negative images. For positive images, stronger biospheric values predicted more pleasant and more activating responses, whereas higher risk perception predicted lower activation. This balanced, context-matched image database provides a standardized resource for studying how affective responses to environmental imagery may shape risk perception and…

items.title: Climate-transition narratives and downside tail risk in carbon and energy markets: evidence from a GARCH-MIDAS framework
From digital skilling to sustainable performance: How climate entrepreneurship and attitudes toward artificial intelligence shape the future of SME technological transitions
items.summary_raw: Digital technologies are reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies respond to environmental pressure, yet two questions remain open. Research linking digital skilling to sustainability has largely tested direct effects without tracing the behavioral pathway such an effect would have to travel, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence have rarely been examined as a condition governing whether green entrepreneurial activity converts into performance. This study addresses both. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, and Contingency Theory into a single explanatory sequence, it models climate entrepreneurship (CE), green entrepreneurial behavior (GEB), and green entrepreneurial intention (GEI) as the mechanisms linking digital entrepreneurial education and training (DEET) to sustainable environmental performance (SEP) and sustainable organizational performance (SOP), with commitment to the environment (CTE) and attitude toward artificial intelligence (ATAI) as boundary conditions. Survey data from 648 Pakistani SMEs are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with a random forest robustness check confirming that the modelled relationships are linear and compensatory. DEET directly predicts organizational performance but has no significant direct effect on environmental performance; its environmental influence is transmitted entirely through the three behavioral mechanisms…

items.title: From catastrophe to efficacy: a longitudinal analysis of The New York Times ’ visual and narrative climate framing on Facebook (2013–2023)
items.summary_raw: This study examines how The New York Times packaged climate-related journalism on Facebook from 2013 to 2023. Using a stratified random sample of 650 posts, the present study applies O’Neill et al.’s climate-frame typology and codes dominant frame, emotional valence, visual-asset format, and central human depiction. Chi-square tests and logistic regressions show significant temporal changes within this single outlet-platform case. Disaster and Moral/Ethics frames declined, whereas Opportunity frames increased; Political/Ideological Struggle remained stable. Standard press photography became less prevalent, while data graphics, text-overlay graphics, and other non-photographic assets became more common. Images centered on political elites declined, while those centered on affected citizens increased. These findings document a production-side shift toward more response-oriented and visually self-contained climate-post packaging, although they do not demonstrate that Facebook caused the changes, that the formats or frames improved performance, or that audiences experienced greater engagement or efficacy. This study contributes a bounded longitudinal baseline for comparative, platform-sensitive, and audience-centered climate-communication research.

items.title: Becoming climate sentinels
items.summary_raw: Abstract In South Korea, forest scientists refashion themselves as “climate sentinels” as they confront subtle yet disquieting shifts in plant seasonality brought about by climate change. Unlike traditional sentinels, who watch for external threats from a frontier, climate sentinels face ecological anomalies and surprises—such as untimely flowering—that have permeated everyday spaces. To register such ecological perplexities, they engage in technoscientific entrainments: deliberate, disciplinary, and laborious coordinations of human observers, trees, protocols, institutions, and modular devices into a shared rhythm of attention. These experimental processes redistribute the traditional embodied technique of mokch’ŭk (eye observation) across nationwide phenological observation networks while reanimating the ecological significance of plant seasonality. For these sentinels, confronting climate change requires attending not only to satellites and heavily computed models but also to the distributed, more‐than‐human experiments through which ecological perplexities are made sensible on the ground.

items.title: Europe pushes tougher line on Russia in growing split with Trump
items.summary_raw: EU leaders are calling for new measures against Moscow as Washington eases off, exposing a widening divide over how to end the war in Ukraine.
